#827. Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend

Lampard appreciation at Everton, Glasner sparking Forest fire, Zubimendi and Kroupi in spotlight and Carrick v Emery

Nothing better encapsulates the dysfunction that was Everton under Farhad Moshiri than the idea that an unknown vandal with a can of spray paint could influence the club’s managerial direction. “Pereira out, Lampard in” they daubed on a wall at Goodison Park when it appeared Vítor Pereira was in line to replace Rafael Benítez in 2022. Alarmed by fan protests, the Everton board opted instead for Frank Lampard and, while his tenure ended 12 months later with the club immersed in another relegation battle, there will be appreciation for the Coventry manager when he makes a first visit to Hill Dickinson Stadium on Friday. The connection between Lampard and Evertonians was genuine and a factor in keeping the club up in 2022. Both parties will be glad to see the other emerging stronger from those troubled times. Jack Grealish, meanwhile, will again be absent for Everton after his recent disciplinary breach, although the manager, David Moyes, said: “We will be working again with Jack soon.” Andy Hunter

Everton v Coventry City, Friday 8pm (all times GMT)

Back in September, when Leeds thrashed Newcastle 4-1 at Elland Road, talk of European qualification filled the West Yorkshire airwaves. Since then Daniel Farke’s side have drawn three and lost two of their ensuing Premier League games, scoring just two goals along the way. Given that their final pass has persistently let them down, optimism is turning to pessimism. Farke would call it realism. The German – who could probably do without facing Roberto De Zerbi’s improving Tottenham on Saturday – is confident his side are making progress but knows they cannot expect to run before properly mastering the art of walking. “We don’t have the individual quality [of the Premier League’s leading teams],” said Farke on Thursday. “We have to compensate by being tactically spot on and good at winning second balls. It’s not a criticism of my players, it’s reality. The dream of Europe is allowed but we know our main aim is to reach 40 points as quickly as possible.” Louise Taylor

Martín Zubimendi has yet to start a Premier League game this season after falling down the pecking order at Arsenal and the Spain midfielder is likely to be the subject of speculation that he could seek to depart in January. The emergence of Myles Lewis-Skelly as an alternative in the No 6 position at the end of last season has had an impact on Zubimendi after he had been a regular starter for most of his debut campaign in the Premier League. The 27-year-old signed from Real Sociedad for around £55m 15 months ago and Mikel Arteta has insisted he remains an integral part of his plans. But with the Arsenal manager trying to find the right balance in his midfield after the arrival of Bruno Guimarães, Zubimendi will be hoping he gets another chance to stake his claim against Hull on Saturday after starting in the narrow win over Slavia Prague in midweek. Ed Aarons

Álvaro Arbeloa is proof that a struggling young manager working in England for the first time can bounce back after a difficult start. Arbeloa was sliding towards the sack a month ago but he has responded at Fulham, who have taken seven points from their last three games, and will hope to extend the unbeaten run when Matthias Jaissle’s inconsistent Newcastle visit Craven Cottage. It is an inviting fixture for Fulham and a big one for Newcastle, who were poor when they lost to Everton on Monday. Jaissle, hired as Eddie Howe’s replacement in the summer, is already under pressure. But the 38-year-old could take inspiration from how Arbeloa has given himself breathing space at Fulham. Jacob Steinberg

Oliver Glasner has previous. He led Wolfsburg from mid-table to the Champions League but fell out with the club hierarchy and left in 2021. Glasner next guided Eintracht Frankfurt to Europa League glory but was openly critical of the squad’s imbalance and quality in four separate outbursts and departed in 2023. His time at Crystal Palace was a great success but after accusing the Eagles’ board in January of “abandoning” his team with the sale of Marc Guéhi to Manchester City, the Austrian left this summer for Nottingham Forest, where he became the fifth head coach in less than a year. You can probably guess where this is going. After Saturday’s defeat by Brentford left Forest 19th, Glasner was typically abrasive: “If the players buy in [to my methods], I think we can have a turnaround. And if not, the sixth manager will come in.” We’ll soon find out if Glasner has won the players around with City visiting Nottingham this weekend. If Forest’s woeful form continues, Glasner may either walk or get his marching orders from trigger-happy owner Evangelos Marinakis. Michael Butler

Nottingham Forest v Manchester City, 5.30pm

Pierre Sage pulled no punches in his assessment of Eddie Nketiah’s career after his excellent winning goal against Fulham last week in the EFL Cup. “I think his potential is higher than his performance for the moment,” said the Crystal Palace manager. “And we have to reduce this gap – because he needs it, the team needs it.” Nketiah is now 27 and won his solitary senior cap for England in 2023 after becoming the record scorer for the under-21s while he was still at Arsenal. His chances of adding to that look unlikely these days having been relegated to third-choice striker at Selhurst Park behind Jean-Philippe Mateta and Jørgen Strand Larsen. But with Mateta suspended for three matches after Palace’s appeal over his red card against Tottenham was rejected, Sunday’s meeting with Liverpool could be another chance for Nketiah to show his ability after scoring a late winner against them in Palace’s thrilling win over Arne Slot’s side last year. EA

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

It has been three weeks since Brighton’s fans were savouring a famous 5-0 thrashing of arch-rivals Crystal Palace at the Amex. But the quirks of the fixture list meant that Fabian Hürzeler’s side played five successive games on the road since then, including two trips to face Manchester City. While they lost some of the momentum from the Palace victory in the defeat by Liverpool at Anfield, last week’s Premier League win over City showed they are serious contenders for the top four and perhaps even more. But Brentford’s visit to the south coast should provide a real test of those credentials as the owner, Tony Bloom, renews his rivalry with his west London counterpart Matthew Benham, who traditionally eschews his seat in the directors’ box for one in the away section. EA

Eli Junior Kroupi did not take the headlines in Bournemouth’s win over Leeds but his cheeky nutmeg and sumptuous no-look pass to set up Amine Adli for the Cherries’ second goal was a reminder of why the youngster continues to be linked with a move to Arsenal, Bayern and PSG, despite being sidelined recently. Kroupi scored 13 Premier League goals last season – only Ryan Giggs, Wayne Rooney, Michael Owen and Romelu Lukaku have reached that total as teenagers – and only Erling Haaland and Will Osula enjoyed a better goal-per-game ratio in 2025-26. Kroupi’s foot injury, sustained in pre-season, has been carefully managed but after three substitute appearances in the wins over Manchester United, Aston Villa and Leeds, will Marco Rose be tempted to start Kroupi at Ipswich? Evanilson is in red hot form as the central striker but Kroupi is just as comfortable as a No 10 and surely has to play if he is fit as Bournemouth chase a seventh consecutive win in all competitions. MB

It is not quite six months since Sunderland beat Chelsea 2-1 at the Stadium of Light and qualified for Europe for the first time in 53 years. A day when Régis Le Bris’s side eclipsed the Club World Cup holders and Enzo Le Fée upstaged Enzo Fernández concluded with Sunderland finishing seventh. During the prolonged post-match celebrations, the captain, Granit Xhaka, grabbed a microphone and declared: “This is just the beginning – we want more.” Fast forward to gloomy November and it is not quite working out like that with even the excitement of next month’s trip to Milan overshadowed by anxiety. Sunderland are bottom of the Premier League, Le Bris concedes his side are in a relegation fight and Xhaka has looked a shadow of his former self ever since Chelsea tried and failed to sign him in the summer. Is Xhaka capable of turning back time? Sunderland securing just a second league win of the season depends on it. Louise Taylor

Can Manchester United win two games of football on the bounce for the first time this season? Being able to pose this question sums up the state Michael Carrick and his side are in as they seek to build on Tuesday’s chaotic comeback victory over Roma. Aston Villa arrive five points better off than their hosts and are everything United are not: stable, upwardly mobile and boasting a manager in Unai Emery who consistently improves players and yields results. As the international break beckons after this last Premier League fixture of the weekend, will Carrick survive what could be an eighth loss in 15 matches? Possibly, if it is not another humiliation, but the truth may be that even United’s erratic executives do not currently know the answer. Jamie Jackson

Manchester United v Aston Villa, Sunday 4.30pm

#826. A bitter end for Ronaldo - the icon who transformed Portugal

Cristiano Ronaldo's old rival Leo Messi left Argentina less than a month ago with a nation applauding him.

The Portugal legend has gone another way, and it was always going to be the case.

The 41-year-old announced his international retirement after 23 years but also after a fallout with coach Jorge Jesus which was resolved with a sanction of 30 days, that had already been served, and a fine of 255 euros.

It was the punishment imposed on the Portuguese striker for leaving the team's training camp without permission. Jesus kept him on the bench for one match and said he did not plan to start him in the next, so Ronaldo went home.

His last appearance came on 24 September against Wales. He ends his international career with 146 goals in 234 games.

A message went around Portugal with a big thank you for everything, calling Ronaldo a global ambassador and an inspiration to millions. Even so, the way it ended leaves a bit of a bitter taste.

Was he going to be named in the next squad? Possibly, as Jesus said the door was open and the decision was Ronaldo's. What is clear is that he was no longer an automatic starter, and Cristiano has never handled that well.

So is this another hissy fit? Partly, yes. He reacted the way he always has when a coach questions his place. But the label hides how much he adapted over the years.

Such a pattern appears with almost every man who sat on the Portuguese bench - there were clashes, but also communion with managers and team-mates that help explain this ending.

Six tournaments, 11 goals - Ronaldo's World Cup legacy

Ronaldo's most iconic moments as he retires from international football

What legacy does Cristiano Ronaldo leave on the international stage?

When a young Ronaldo first joined the squad, he arrived at camp with his baseball cap on backwards, enormous sunglasses and headphones turned up so loud they could be heard from a distance.

He would not take the cap off to eat among veterans like Luis Figo and Rui Costa. Luiz Felipe Scolari saw an extraordinary player who was immature and obsessed with showing off. He reprimanded him in public, then told him privately that if he changed his attitude, he would one day captain Portugal.

The first great disappointment came early, and it came at home. At 19, Ronaldo played in the final of Euro 2004 at the Estadio da Luz in Lisbon, in front of a country that had convinced itself the trophy was already on its way.

A single headed goal by Angelos Charisteas was enough for unfancied Greece to win it by surprise. When the final whistle went, Ronaldo could not hold back the tears, and the image of the teenager crying on his own pitch travelled everywhere.

It was a painful way to learn what a final costs, and it left him with a hunger that never really went away.

Figo owned the number 7 at the time, so Ronaldo had to have 17. Figo helped him settle but had no intention of making it easy. When he left the national team in 2006, the shirt and the team became Ronaldo's.

In September 2005, before a qualifier in Russia, Scolari and Figo went to his room to tell him his father had died. Scolari offered to send him home. Ronaldo chose to play, asked his team-mates to behave as normal, and spent time in the dressing room doing ball tricks.

That was his way to cope with the expected but still hugely hurtful passing of his alcoholic dad. He later called Scolari "father". That way the national team had become the place that held him together.

Things went sour with Carlos Queiroz. After the 2010 World Cup exit against Spain, asked to explain a poor performance, Ronaldo told journalists to ask the coach. His influence in the camp had grown so large it changed routines and habits, which explains why the coach felt undermined.

The sociologist Joao Nuno Coelho offers the best lens on how Portugal sees him. In his analysis, the national team became a representation of Portuguese identity and of the country's need to be seen internationally.

In years of economic hardship and a crisis of confidence, a team that won admiration abroad was important beyond football.

Ronaldo stood at the centre of that need and created contradictory feelings. Some Portuguese questioned his individualism and his ego, and not everyone saw themselves in his personality.

Coelho explains criticising him became more difficult as time went by. The country wanted to be proud of him and sometimes felt uneasy at the same time.

The former international Jorge Andrade told me some supporters preferred figures like Figo, Eusebio, Paulo Futre or Rui Costa. Even so, Portugal was proud to have him. And with the titles, the doubts eased.

Under Fernando Santos in 2016, he changed. He accepted playing as a centre forward next to Nani - he had never taken a coach's instructions so naturally.

After the opening draw with Iceland, he told Nani in private that he trusted Santos, and the dressing room began to see a real captain. After missing a penalty against Austria, he barely slept. Santos woke up and found him already awake.

At the training camp in Marcoussis, he took a fan's megaphone and told supporters Portugal had won nothing yet. He was enjoying the leadership role.

In the final in Paris, he left the pitch in tears, injured. He had not had the best tournament, with a muscle complaint that did not let him perform at his best.

Nani took the armband. At half-time Ronaldo pulled himself together to encourage his team-mates, and before extra time, still limping, he told Eder he would score.

But the old instinct never fully disappeared. During extra-time, Ronaldo stood in the technical area giving orders until the fourth official sent him back. Other coaches I consulted found it excessive.

His greatest strength, the need to influence every result, also made limits hard to accept.

When he debuted in 2003, Portugal was still searching for its first major title. Some players mark an era, and others change a national team for good. He belongs to the second group.

That night in July 2016 gave Portugal its first European Championship.

Three years later he scored a hat-trick against Switzerland to put them into the first Nations League final, which Portugal won. In 2025 he lifted a second Nations League at an age when most players have retired.

No one has scored more goals for a national side, and no one has pulled on the Portugal shirt more times.

Under his influence, Portugal stopped being a gifted team and became one that arrives at every tournament expecting to contend, while a whole generation of players came through a dressing room where he decided what the standard was.

Coelho's point holds here as well: a small country found a way to be noticed, and for two decades he was its face.

After 2016 the question around him changed. Fewer asked whether he was selfish, and more asked whether Portugal depended on him too much.

Ronaldo scored 146 goals and won 234 caps for Portugal

In the World Cup in 2018, he scored three against Spain, including a free-kick after 45 attempts in major tournaments, and the team still went out to Uruguay.

After a difficult 2026 World Cup, much was made of him still starting up front when in fact statistically that was his best period.

Under Roberto Martinez, with 28 goals in 37 games, 0.756 per match, improves the 0.624 with Santos.

The federation has announced a special tribute to honour his contribution, and that is necessary as the exit has not left fans room for a celebration they want to be part of.

Not only they grew up with him, he took them to places they had not yet been.

#825. Charlton’s struggles expose ‘absolute ocean’ between WSL and second tier

Pointless after eight games, Karen Hills’ team are struggling to compete against clubs with chunkier wallets

Played eight, lost eight. Welcome to the Women’s Super League, Charlton Athletic, a club in danger of being chewed up, toyed with and spat straight back out by the top tier.

Bruised by their 6-0 defeat against Chelsea on Sunday, last season’s playoff winners are finding WSL life tough, conceding more than three goals per game on average and struggling to compete against clubs with chunkier wallets. But are they underperforming or are they merely the victims of their own success?

Promoted against the odds last season, defying some of the bigger-spending sides in the second tier such as Newcastle and Bristol City, Karen Hills’ team overachieved by eventually beating Leicester on penalties to secure a top-flight spot. And that was the last time they had anything to cheer about. Sunday’s trip to second-bottom Crystal Palace, another of the promoted sides, theoretically offers Charlton one of their better opportunities to match the 2026 UK Eurovision entry Look Mum No Computer and register one point.

Charlton have been unfortunate. The club-record signing, Linda Líf Boama, suffered a serious knee injury in September, while another of their most important additions, the France defender Hawa Cissoko, signed for her top-tier experience, is with an ankle injury. It would, therefore, be wrong to say there was no serious attempt to strengthen the squad before this season, but Charlton’s fellow promoted teams’ summer business was undeniably more ambitious, whether it be Birmingham’s capture of two Manchester United players or Palace signing the former Tottenham captain Bethany England and the WSL2 Golden Boot winner Lexi Lloyd-Smith.

Charlton lost significant cash in WSL2. The club’s financial accounts for the year ending 30 June 2025 – which were filed in October – stated that the women’s team made a loss of £1.32m, that they had net liabilities of £2.18m and that additional funding would be required. Precise details on wage bills, revenue and expenditure were not published after the company was deemed to be entitled to exemption from audit under section 479A of the Companies Act 2006.

Promotion to the WSL also comes with additional expenditure needed to meet enhanced minimum requirements and, not insignificantly, higher minimum salaries. In WSL2 last season, clubs had to pay players aged 23 and over a minimum salary of £26,900; aged 21 and 22 a minimum of £22,200; and those aged 18 to 20 at least £17,500. In the top tier, those minimum salaries rise to £42,500, £34,700 and £26,900 respectively.

Meanwhile, central income is modest; WSL Football’s financial accounts for 2024-25 stated that £9.41m was paid to their 24 member clubs, approximately £400,000 each. Unlike promotion to the men’s top tier, which can transform a club’s financial fortunes, the main benefit of reaching the WSL for a women’s team is the potential for greater exposure on Sky Sports and the BBC’s broadcast coverage. Charlton, it should be noted, also do not have the comfort blanket of a wealthy men’s team owner to invest in their women’s side.

There is a feeling within the women’s game that summer recruitment was somewhat rushed. Their first signing was not announced until 18 July. In contrast, Birmingham’s head coach, Amy Merricks, spoke repeatedly of trying to become “WSL ready” as early as the 2024-25 campaign.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Birmingham and Palace have both drawn at Arsenal this season and caused other sides problems, whereas Charlton – only the fifth team to lose their opening eight WSL games – have struggled to keep the ball, completing only six sequences of 10 or more passes, averaging only a 65% pass accuracy. All three teams, however, are finding the step up to the top tier a challenge and it is not surprising that the WSL’s bottom three are the promoted trio. Merricks, whose team travel to London City Lionesses on Sunday, said on Friday that “the way the table looks now is probably a way off how it will finish” but the gap between the divisions was “an absolute ocean”.

Asked how wide she feels the gulf is, Hills, who says her Charlton players have “prepared really well this week”, replied: “We’re trying to make the jump and trying to stay with this pack. The gap is continuing to get bigger and you see with some of the top teams the players that they’ve brought in and the finances and the resources that they have. It’s going to be a big challenge and we’re finding that out on a weekly basis.”

#823. 'Putting his doubters in their place' - Rooney lands pundit of year award

Wayne Rooney has transitioned to broadcasting following a managerial career with Derby County, DC United, Birmingham City and Plymouth Argyle

"I like a lot of them artists, but I thought it was crap."

Wayne Rooney's assessment of the 2026 World Cup final half-time show - delivered live on BBC Television - was blunt.

The show, which featured Madonna, BTS, Shakira and Justin Bieber, ran to 27 minutes and 22 seconds. Rooney, who played at three World Cups for England, was unimpressed.

It caught some - including fellow pundit Joe Hart - by surprise. But Rooney's plain-speaking and sense of humour through the tournament had connected with viewers.

On Thursday, the former Manchester United and England captain was named pundit of the year at the Broadcast Sport Awards., external

Gabby Logan was named sports presenter of the year for her work across the World Cup, Six Nations, London Marathon, Match of the Day and European Athletics for BBC Sport.

Ed Leigh and Tim Warwood, who worked on Ski Sunday and the Winter Olympics, were given the sports commentator of the year award, while Ultras was named sports documentary of the year (series).

The awards were announced at a ceremony in London attended by 650 people from the sports television industry.

Rooney said: "I didn't realise how tough it was going to be when I first started doing it.

"I've always been my own biggest critic. And even now I need to improve, I need to be better. It's a lot of hard work."

Wayne wasn't holding back about the half-time show

Rooney's move to broadcasting after a stellar playing career - followed by a testing stint as a manager - has not always been smooth.

His debut as a full-time pundit on Match of the Day in August 2025 divided opinion,, external with one fan writing on social media: "Just because you have done something, does not automatically make you good to talk/explain and teach others well."

Guardian journalist Paul MacInnes was more upbeat about Rooney's debut.

"He's articulate, and on Saturday night was able to conjure up the right word when you could see he was looking for it," he wrote., external

"He is tactically insightful and has a wealth of experience to draw from too."

As a player, Rooney learned from managers including Sir Alex Ferguson and David Moyes, and won the Champions League, Europa League, Premier League (five times), FA Cup and League Cup (three times).

He was not always the most articulate in his post-match interviews. As a pundit, he has found his voice.

In an attempt to better himself as a broadcaster, Rooney has sought feedback and advice from experienced television executives, as well as other players-turned-pundits including Alan Shearer, Danny Murphy, Hart and Micah Richards.

"I do look at the other pundits who have been there a long time," added Rooney.

"I see how they do it. I enjoy it, it keeps me involved in football."

Asked about dealing with criticism from people watching him on TV, Rooney responded: "You do see it.

"It drives me to be better. I always feel when I do something I want to do better and be the best I can."

Paul Stretford, Rooney's long-serving agent, said people should not be surprised by what his client can achieve.

"It is no surprise to me that Wayne has continued to put his doubters in their place with his football intelligence and straightforward manner," added Stretford.

"Time and time again as a player he was able to raise his game to incredible levels.

"They should also not be surprised at his drive and ambition to be the best that he can possibly be. And he does this with a combination of intelligence and humility."

Philip Bernie, head of BBC Sport events, said Rooney had shown a "great willingness to learn and determination to improve" as a broadcaster.

"Wayne is also a very likeable guy, a proper team player, with no ego on display," he added.

'One of the worst decisions I've ever seen' - Shearer & Rooney on Digne penalty shout

As well as developing chemistry with his fellow pundits, Rooney has changed his appearance after committing to a healthier lifestyle through a fitness regime which involves games of padel and boxing training.

"Like anyone who cares about their job, Wayne had to work hard - to learn skills around analysis and delivery - and he's improved so much in a short time," said Alex Kay-Jelski, director of BBC Sport.

"Micah and Joe alongside him at the World Cup were perfect team-mates - three equals - and you'll be seeing more of them together on the BBC in coming seasons."

Their chemistry was obvious in the summer, particularly when they swapped their microphones for oars after an erroneous Rooney prediction.

He pledged to row down the River Mersey if Norway beat Brazil, and when they did, he confirmed on air he would adapt the challenge to do it in the United States.

That led to him, Hart and Richards to take to the Hudson River in New York.

"Wayne deserves this so much," added Kay-Jelski. "He's a great mix of incredibly clever, funny in a self-deprecating manner and likeable.

"From a BBC side he's easy to work with, treats everyone the same whether they're a former team-mate or starting out in a junior position, and his words carry real weight."

#822. WNBA Stars Paige Bueckers, Azzi Fudd Confirm Breakup

Dallas Wings’ teammates Paige Bueckers and Azzi Fudd confirmed they broke up “over a year ago” in the WNBA rookie’s podcast Fudd Around and Find Out.

Paige Bueckers and Azzi Fudd pulled a pass fake on WNBA fans.

The Dallas Wings teammates—who confirmed their relationship in July 2025—shared they are no longer together, and haven’t been for over a year.

Welcoming Bueckers to the Nov. 6 episode of her Fudd Around and Find Out podcast, Fudd confirmed the news as the former couple laughed it off, quipping, “I don’t know how else to say that.”

Bueckers also confirmed that the duo—who first sparked romance rumors during their time playing basketball together at University of Connecticut—had been broken up for “over a year.”

In fact, it was well before they knew they would be stepping onto the court together.

“To share that now everybody’s gonna be like, ‘Oh my gosh they’re teammates. How is this going to work?’” Bueckers explained. “We were not together before she got drafted so all those narratives can go to bed. She was not drafted because she was my girlfriend. She was drafted because she deserved it.”

The 25-year-old emphasized that she and Fudd—who was drafted in April—remain friends.

“She’s an amazing human, an amazing basketball player,” she continued. “We’re still friends, we’re still cool. We broke up over a year ago, so we played an entire season together. We’re the utmost professional. We care about basketball.”

Bueckers also acknowledged that she wanted to give a “speech” regarding the fan’s obsession with their romance since it was confirmed.

“There’s a whole list and notes of things that I would love to address if I had the time or the energy but I think and Azzi can agree to this just to start by saying we don’t stand for hate of any kind,” the guard continued. “We don’t condone that. If you’re using our names and our image to spread that, that’s not who we are and that’s not what we’re about.”

Nodding to the negative messages Bueckers and Fudd’s family, friends and teammates received during their relationship, Bueckers acknowledged, “That’s never been something that we’ve stood for.”

Ultimately, both Bueckers and Fudd, 23, made it clear they only support each other—and only want support for each other from their fans.

“We’re still going to be great teammates,” Bueckers continued. “We’re going to be professionals. We are still going to have other friends. We will eventually move on.”

She also didn’t want any hate for their potential future partners joking, “I know we will continue to be outside and be lit and have a good time so we should not get punished for that as well.”

Fudd, for her part, concurred with everything Bueckers laid out, and confirmed they won’t be speaking any further on their relationship.

“We know you guys are probably curious and have a ton of questions,” she acknowledged, “but we’ve addressed everything that we need to and the rest will stay with us.”

For a deeper look into the love lives of WNBA stars, keep reading…

Still, there have been definitive clues that the Bayou Barbie has found her Ken in Orlando Magic center Wendell Carter Jr. "That’s a sign," the Atlanta Dream power forward captioned a TikTok showcasing an impressive arrangements of roses, "that’s a signnnn." And it was certainly a big play when the Duke alum turned up to the 2025 WNBA All-Star game sporting a t-shirt baring Reese's visage.

The NCAA champ—set to appear on season two of The Hunting Wives—returned the favor, attending a December 2025 Magic game in a jersey emblazoned with the words "My Man."

Game recognizes game, and three-time WNBA champion A'ja Wilson has found her ace of hearts in Bam Adebayo.

The low-key couple first sparked dating rumors in the summer of 2024, and Wilson confirmed their romance with a bit of a pump fake when she showed up at NBA All Star Weekend in February 2025.

"My NBA All-Star is not here," the Las Vegas Aces center told People, acknowledging that the Miami Heat center hadn't made the roster. But Adebayo was busy "getting the rest he needs," she added, "and that's the best Valentine gift that I can truly give him, is just the rest."

And they're only heating up, Adebayo showing up to support Wilson—who made her fifth straight All-Star team—during the WNBA All-Star festivities in July 2025.

Months later, in her TIME Athlete of the Year cover story, she revealed they'd actually been huddled up way longer than fans realized, making that first move at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021.

Next up: Adding to their squad. "That is always a dream," she said of having kids with Adebayo. "This is my life partner. Honestly, what on earth was my world before you? That’s how much he’s impacted my life, my family’s life."

Sabrina Ionescu has racked up an impressive haul of trophies playing for the New York Liberty, WNBA All-Stars and U.S. Olympic team, but the day she married NFL player Hroniss Grasu is especially close to her heart.

"March 10, 2024. The day I got to marry my best friend, my other half," she captioned her Instagram wedding photo. "The best day of my life."

Marta Xargay Casademont & Breanna Stewart

Three-time WNBA champion Breanna Stewart met her love match with Spanish basketball player Marta Xargay Casademont. They connected as teammates on a Russian professional women's basketball team in 2018 and got engaged and married in 2021. They welcomed their first child Ruby in August 2021, followed by their son Theo in October 2023.

Xargay Casademont retired from the sport in 2021, but continues to support her wife's career, writing on Instagram after Stewart's New York Liberty won the 2024 Finals, "So freaking proud of you!"

Indiana Fever megastar Caitlin Clark has been dating basketball player and former Butler University assistant coach Connor McCaffery since April 2023.

The pair haven't been shy about celebrating their love on social media, with McCaffery posting a sweet birthday tribute for his girlfriend's January 2025 birthday: "You have an incredible ability to inspire and lift up those around you, and I am lucky to learn from you every day. Thank you for always being you. I love you."

New York Liberty shooting guard and 2021 WNBA All-Star Betnijah Laney is married to fellow basketball player Jordan Hamilton, who started for the Denver Nuggets, New Orleans Pelicans, and Houston Rockets during his NBA career.

In an Instagram tribute for their second wedding anniversary in 2023, Laney wrote, "Your arms are my favorite place to be."

After dating for eight years, Diana Taurasi married her Phoenix Mercury teammate Penny Taylor on May 13, 2017. Now both retired from the sport, the iconic WNBA couple have more time to spend with their children, Leo and Isla.

After a few weeks of speculation, Dallas Wings point guard Paige Bueckers confirmed in July 2025 that she was dating Azzi Fudd, her former teammate on the UConn’s women’s basketball team.

And with Fudd selected first overall by the Wings in the 2026 draft, the two were thrilled to pair up on and off the hardwood. "I'm excited to play again with Paige," Fudd told ESPN during draft night April 13. "She's an incredible person. An incredible player, and it's gonna be a lot of fun."

In November 2026, though, the couple confirmed they had broken up "over a year" prior.

"We’re still friends, we’re still cool," Bueckers explained during an appearance on Fudd's Fudd Around and Find Out podcast. "We broke up over a year ago, so we played an entire season together. We’re the utmost professional. We care about basketball.”

Prior to playing for the Indiana Fever in 2024 and re-joining the Seattle Storm in February 2025, Katie Lou Samuelson was busy with her life off the court. She married basketball player Devin Cannady in April 2023 and the couple announced the birth of their daugher Aliya in August 2023.

WNBA superstar Napheesa Collier can add devoted wife and mom to her long list of achievements (which includes two Olympic gold medals and 2025 All-Star Game MVP).

In October 2019, the Minnesota Lynx forward got engaged to basketball skills coach Alex Bazzell and they were married three years later. In 2022, they welcomed daughter Mila Sarah Bazzell.

Then-Chicago Sky teammates Allie Quigley and Courtney Vandersloot were married in December 2018 and share daughter Jana, who was born on April 8, 2025.

The winning pair are not only the first married couple to win a professional sports championship together (the 2021 WNBA Finals), but in May 2025, a month before Quigley announced her retirement, Vandersloot surpassed her wife's record as the all-time leading scorer for the Chicago Sky.

In March 2021, Alyssa Thomas shared on social media that she was dating her then-Connecticut Sun teammate, DeWanna Bonner.

The pair got engaged in 2023 when Thomas proposed during the WNBA All-Star Weekend. Bonner is also mom to Cali and Demi, the twins she welcomed in 2017 with ex-wife and former Phoenix Mercury teammate Candice Dupree.

#821. Thierno Barry double fires Everton to comeback win against Coventry

The wildly optimistic Evertonian – if such a being exists – could not have envisaged David Moyes’ side fifth in the Premier League with Thierno Barry just behind Erling Haaland in the goalscoring chart when their transfer window closed in calamitous fashion. Yet there they sit, team and striker defying all expectations, following a stirring comeback against luckless Coventry.

Frank Lampard endured a torturous night against his old club as Coventry impressed but were refused two strong penalty claims. The Coventry manager felt his team were denied a third time by the video assistant referee for an apparent handball by Barry when edging Everton ahead. Replays were inconclusive. It was the dancing French forward’s second goal of the game and 10th in all competitions this season. He also delivered a fine assist for Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall as the in-form midfielder put his latest England disappointment behind him to seal victory in convincing style.

It was a landmark occasion for Moyes as he equalled the great Harry Catterick’s record of 592 games in charge of Everton. “Seeing my name alongside Harry Catterick’s is hugely humbling and I hope I can continue to add to that figure,” the Scot wrote in his programme notes. “What I really hope, though, is that I can bring trophies to the club like Harry Catterick did.” Equalling Catterick’s collection of two league titles and an FA Cup may be beyond Moyes, who is in the final year of his Everton contract and working in very different times, but what he is doing with the smallest squad in the Premier League ranks as an achievement itself.

The Everton manager said post-match: “It’s great if I can build expectations because that means we are doing well but at some point someone is going to say ‘Look at the size of their squad’ and you might have to calm down. It might catch up with us at some point but I have to say the boys are doing really well.”

Moyes’ team laboured until falling behind to Yann Gboho’s opener early in the second half. From that moment they roused themselves and showed the clinical touch and smart decision-making that eluded Coventry, but luck was also on their side.

James Tarkowski survived two penalty appeals in one go when leaping between Caleb Yirenkyi and Ethan Pinnock to clear a Coventry free-kick. The Everton captain appeared to pull the former’s hair and raise an arm towards the latter’s face. Neither the referee, Stuart Attwell, nor the VAR, Timothy Wood, considered the hair-pull had met this season’s higher threshold for excessive force. Last season Tarkowski would have been sent off.

Lampard said: “The rules are fine. It’s not a red card and I kind of get that, but the rule remains it’s a foul so I felt it was a foul.” Coventry were denied a second penalty claim when Taiwo Awoniyi went down under a challenge from Vitalii Mykolenko. “Taiwo is on the line of the box and it is a penalty,” said Lampard. “I thought it was a penalty by the time Myko’s knee was in the back of Taiwo’s knee.”

Coventry finally, deservedly, got a break when benefiting from some abysmal Everton defending to take the lead. The influential Jack Rudoni was involved with a pass into Gboho who, with the aid of a deflection off Tarkowski, easily held off Merlin Röhl, Harrison Armstrong and Jarrad Branthwaite before poking a shot past the unsighted Jordan Pickford.

Less than 10 minutes later, and to general astonishment, Lampard’s team were behind. Tyler Dibling had been quiet on his first league start of the season but was involved in the Everton equaliser with a dangerous cross from the right. Coventry failed to clear and when Mykolenko swept in a cross at the second attempt Barry, showing good strength to hold off Jay Dasilva, beat Carl Rushworth with an emphatic header.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

The French striker soon reached double figures for the campaign when bundling home Tyrique George’s delivery to the far post. Dasilva made a mess of his attempted clearance and headed the ball against Barry – his hand, possibly – before it spun past Rushworth and over the line.

There was no questioning the legitimacy of Barry’s next goal involvement. The confident striker split the Coventry defence with a superb pass into Dewsbury-Hall, who ended his disappointing day on a high by racing clear and beating Rushworth with a precise finish inside the keeper’s near post.

Moyes called Barry’s display “fabulous”. He expanded: “Haaland’s worried about him catching him now! I don’t see many young centre-forwards scoring loads of goals in the Premier League. He’s settled down a bit more now. His language, his understanding and his communication is much better as well. Obviously he’s working hard to get in those positions to score. I’m really pleased for him.”

#820. Talking points as Premiership prepares for international break

Ivor Pandur and Jacob Chapman both made big saves the last time Rangers and St Mirren met

The Scottish Premiership resumes for one more round of fixtures before this month's international break.

Six games, five kick-off times, lots of issues to address.

Last weekend turned out to be a good one for Rangers in more ways than one.

A late Ryan Naderi goal sealed a Premier Sports Cup semi-final win over Aberdeen on Saturday evening.

And, on Sunday at lunchtime, Premiership leaders Celtic lost in Falkirk, opening up the possibility of Rangers reducing the gap at the top to a point before the reigning champions host Kilmarnock on Sunday.

However, to do that, Derek McInnes' side, now unbeaten in 11 outings, must win away to St Mirren on Saturday.

The last time Rangers were in the Saturday 20:00 slot, they dropped two points away to Dundee and another warning for the Ibrox side is St Mirren's recent home form - a draw with Hibernian and a victory over in-form Dundee.

Craig McLeish's side have won just once in eight games but ran Rangers pretty close the last time the sides met in Glasgow, only a late Bojan Miovski goal separating the sides.

The Buddies are holding their own in the Premiership this term, sitting eighth within touching distance of the top six at this early stage and St Mirren led Celtic in a Saturday night contest before eventually losing 2-1 in early September.

An intriguing match under the lights awaits.

'I love these kind of things' - Reedijk on spin-tingling rendition of Sunshine on Leith

Hibs were the other League Cup semi-final victors, coming from a goal down to beat Edinburgh rivals Heart of Midlothian 2-1 to end a seven-game run without a win.

The task for Marink Reedijk and his side now is to get their Premiership form in order before returning to Hampden to face Rangers in mid-December.

Under their new Dutch coach, Hibs have taken only one point from a possible 12 so far and prop up the table having played 11 games.

Aberdeen host the Edinburgh side on Saturday evening and the Dons themselves need a turnaround in fortunes in the league, having lost two in a row in the division prior to their semi-final defeat by Rangers.

Stephen Robinson's side are third from bottom, three points better off than Hibs, and the sides drew 1-1 at Easter Road only last month.

It's perhaps still a tad early to be talking in terms of crisis for either club, particularly given Hibs could end the calendar year with a trophy in the cabinet, but both teams need to get a bit of a move on to preserve their top-six ambitions.

Duran & Osmand spark Celtic into life - but where does that leave Hogh?

Late Duran double downs Besiktas to give Celtic first Europa League win

Injury-hit and error-ridden Hearts slump to defeat in Thun

Last week's Saturday results in the Premiership did little to break up the clutch of clubs jostling for position in the middle of the table.

It could be a similar story this weekend with Dundee United hosting Motherwell and a Tayside derby between St Johnstone and Dundee, with both at 15:00 GMT on Saturday.

Well ended their long wait for a win by beating St Mirren at home last weekend while St Johnstone twice fought back with 10 players to draw 2-2 with Kilmarnock as the Dundee duo had the weekend off.

Motherwell's 3-0 win over United in early September is their biggest of the league season so far, the visitors having played most of that match with 10 men.

The same day, Dundee thought they were on their way to three points when they led late on against Saints at Dens, but the Perth side had other ideas with an even later equaliser.

With Dundee one point behind Falkirk and United one point further back, both have the chance to move above the Bairns before they face Hearts on Sunday.

'Celtic character shone through big time' - O'Neill

Celtic bounced back from defeat by Falkirk with a stirring 3-2 victory at home to Besiktas in the Europa League.

Earlier on Thursday, injury ravaged Hearts lost 3-1 to Thun in Switzerland.

As such, both Scottish sides play their Premiership fixtures on Sunday.

Rangers' result the night before will either offer encouragement or added pressure, with leaders Celtic four points clear of Rangers and the same margin of points between second place and Hearts as things stand.

With one win now in seven games and with 10 first-team players missing on Thursday, Wouter Vrancken and his squad are desperate for the respite provided by the international break.

First, though, they must host in-form Falkirk, who are bidding for five wins in a row. The Bairns' first league win of the campaign was at home to Hearts back in mid-September. They have seldom looked back.

By half-time at Tynecastle, Celtic will be getting ready to kick off against Kilmarnock. Misfiring Kasper Hogh's only three Celtic goals so far came in a 5-1 win at Rugby Park back in August.

Fellow summer signing Camilo Duran has done most of the scoring for Celtic since, including a double (a Duran Duran if you will) against Besiktas.

Whoever starts in attack for the hosts, second-bottom Killie will have their work cut out to improve a run of one win in six outings.

#819. James out for minimum of five games - Bompastor

James was substituted in the 6-0 win at Charlton last weekend

Chelsea manager Sonia Bompastor says Lauren James will be out for at least the next few weeks, casting doubt on her availability for England's World Cup qualifying play-off matches.

The 25-year-old will miss at least the next five matches for the Blues, including Everton's visit to Stamford Bridge on Saturday and a crucial match against champions Manchester City next weekend.

It also casts doubt on her chances of being available for England's World Cup qualifying play-off matches against Ukraine in December.

After James came off in distress in the 35th minute of the 6-0 win over Charlton Athletic, Bompastor confirmed the injury: "The only one who will be missing is LJ.

"She had a scan and she has an injury in her hamstring, so we won't see her until the end of this block."

There was more positive news for Chelsea, with midfielder Lexi Potter, who made her England debut last month, back after missing the trip to Charlton.

Chelsea, meanwhile, are top of the WSL table having won matches both with and without James this season.

Bompastor added: "Of course we know how good Lauren is for us and for the team.

"Also, my job is to make sure I find solutions when some players are not available and not playing for the team. I think the good thing is that when I looked at some of the statistics from last week, we are a team who are able to score through different players.

"The last game we had against Charlton, a lot of players were involved in scoring again. Also, I think every player on the pitch had a shot on goal.

"Even if it was not always a great one, at least all of the players who were on the pitch had a shot on goal. I think that's a good thing and, again, my job now is to make sure I find the solutions without LJ on the pitch."

#818. Bellinghams celebrate ‘beautiful story’ as Jobe joins Jude in Tuchel’s England 2.0

Jude had asked head coach to scout Dortmund midfielder

‘It will be beautiful for Jude to have his brother close’

Thomas Tuchel has given a first England call-up to Jobe Bellingham, admitting the midfielder’s older brother, Jude, had nagged him to do so, as he set up the prospect of their family dream being realised.

Tuchel’s inclusion of the younger Bellingham for the Nations League games against Croatia and Spain was further evidence of his shift away from the squad that served him well at the World Cup last summer and towards a fresh dynamic for the mission to win Euro 2028. The manager has named a 25-man group for the game against Croatia at Wembley on Thursday and the one against Spain in Madrid three days after; of the 22 outfield players, only 11 were at the World Cup.

Jobe Bellingham, the England Under-21s captain, has impressed for Borussia Dortmund this season and Jude is on record as saying how much it would mean if they could play together for their country, especially at a major tournament. “It would be the biggest dream of my life,” he said. “It would mean more than any of the trophies I have won.”

Tuchel said the brothers coming together in his England squad was a “beautiful story” and he wondered whether Jobe’s presence could inspire Jude to even greater heights. “Let’s see what the effect is,” Tuchel said. “Jude always behaves like a big brother, taking care of his younger brother. I think that helps Jobe now in camp. And it will be beautiful for Jude to have his brother close.

“Me and Jude spoke about his brother because I was aware it was always his dream [to play for England with Jobe]. Jude was always like: ‘Watch him, watch him, he’s good, he can make it.’ I would say: ‘Yeah, we are watching him.’ And we know, of course, [about him] from Lee Carsley [the under-21s manager].”

Tuchel described Jobe as “maybe more a No 8 than a classic 6 and less of a 10”. He noted that with Myles Lewis-Skelly suspended against Croatia, Jobe’s chances of being involved were higher. It has been 19 years since Gary and Phil Neville were the last brothers to play together for England.

Tuchel accidentally referred to Jobe as “Jube” at one point, a slip that will doubtless be made by others, and said it was a special moment to break the news of the call-up to him on a video call. “He couldn’t stop smiling,” Tuchel said. “He has the same beautiful smile as Jude.”

It is clear that Tuchel’s relationship with Jude Bellingham is on a secure footing, as opposed to this time last year when the player’s place in the squad was in doubt – and certainly his spot in the XI. “It was a bit of an up and down [relationship] but we are in a good place,” Tuchel said. “I hope we have finished with the down. You never know as a coach!”

Goalkeepers Jordan Pickford (Everton), Jason Steele (Brighton), James Trafford (Leeds United)

Defenders Trent Alexander-Arnold (Real Madrid), Jarrad Branthwaite (Everton), Marc Guéhi (Manchester City), Lewis Hall (Newcastle United), Ezri Konsa (Arsenal), Jarell Quansah (Bayer Leverkusen), Djed Spence (Inter), Ben White (Arsenal)

Midfielders Elliot Anderson (Manchester City), Jobe Bellingham (Borussia Dortmund), Jude Bellingham (Real Madrid), James Garner (Everton), Josh King (Fulham), Myles Lewis-Skelly (Arsenal), Declan Rice (Arsenal)

Forwards Dominic Calvert-Lewin (Leeds United), Eberechi Eze (Arsenal), Morgan Gibbs-White (Nottingham Forest), Anthony Gordon (Barcelona), Harry Kane (Bayern Munich), Rio Ngumoha (Liverpool), Morgan Rogers (Chelsea)

More broadly, Tuchel looked reinvigorated after the success of the September/October camp when his team won three out of four Nations League ties to all but guarantee a place in the quarter-finals. Tuchel had been tense at the start of the get-together as he was assailed by the fallout from the World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina.

He made some ruthless decisions in September, discarding Noni Madueke, Ollie Watkins and Ivan Toney from the squad he took to the World Cup. Dean Henderson, Dan Burn and Jordan Henderson, picked in the summer and fit again, have been left out, while Kobbie Mainoo and Nico O’Reilly, who is a managing an injury, were also not selected. He overlooked Cole Palmer and Phil Foden. Missing through injury are Reece James, Tino Livramento, John Stones, Trevoh Chalobah, Alex Scott, Bukayo Saka and Marcus Rashford.

Tuchel has placed an emphasis on youth in his post-World Cup selections and he added Josh King to the squad on Friday. The 19-year-old attacking midfielder’s only previous involvement was at the pre-World Cup training camp in Florida. Tuchel has also given a recall to the more experienced right-back Ben White.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

It was put to Tuchel that his squad had the look of an England 2.0. “It has to be like this,” he said. “We said at some point that we need to take the next step, otherwise you’re left behind. You need to bring in new players for competition; young players, fresh energy. I was a bit worried in the last camp because we were missing so many internal leaders but the group did excellently in a new style, in a new leadership way but in their style. Now there’s a little bit of proof of concept. We give the players the opportunity and responsibility.”

Tuchel namechecked his current leaders as Harry Kane, Saka, Jude Bellingham, Elliot Anderson, Declan Rice, Ezri Konsa and Marc Guéhi. He said he had spoken to them on day one of the last camp – although not Rice, because he had withdrawn – about the need for them “to make sure we have the same standards as at the World Cup”.

Were the seven players the leadership group? “Per se,” Tuchel replied. “I said straight away that I want to have a group that starts matches regularly. These were the players – without having a guarantee. But I said: ‘I want you to start these matches and you make sure that the energy, attitude, the standards within the group are at the highest level.’ That has not changed. So they are basically a leadership group on the field.”

Tuchel said Palmer’s exclusion was “not personal … but the competition is on. It’s about the ones who walk the walk and come to camp”. He made it sound as if Foden was closer to a recall.

“Phil is always an option because I’m in love with him as a player,” Tuchel said. “It was very close. It’s also close for Eberechi Eze to keep his place with us. He’s not starting for Arsenal. The advantage was maybe that Eberechi and Morgan Gibbs-White were in camp last time. They need to fight for it. That’s what we want. And Phil is always close.”

Tuchel also commented on Mainoo’s omission. He took the midfielder to the World Cup but did not play him. “He was hugely disappointed from the World Cup and deservedly so,” Tuchel said. “I said in front of the team and the staff: ‘Sorry, I didn’t pick you. You did nothing wrong. That is on me.’ I think it cost him a bit of confidence. Then he pulled out of the last camp when I was desperate to include him in this new start. And then he entered a difficult spell. He was injured and Man United fell off a cliff a little bit performance-wise.”

#817. Serbian police shoot dead assailant at Israeli Embassy

A "minor" has been killed by police after attacking a guard at Israel's embassy in Belgrade with knives, the interior minister says. Ivica Dacic said police had declared the highest terror alert after the incident.

A knife-wielding assailant attacked a police guard outside the Israeli Embassy in the Serbian capital, Belgrade, overnight to Wednesday, slightly wounding the officer before being shot dead by him, Serbia's interior minister said.

Interior Minister Ivica Dacic said the attacker, whom he described as a minor, had been monitored by security agencies as a supporter of the terrorist organization "Islamic State" (IS).

Israel's Foreign Ministry later confirmed an "attempted terrorist attack" near its embassy in Belgrade, adding that no personnel were injured and the incident was being investigated.

The attacker was thought to come from the western Serbian town of Sabac and "kept the black flag in support of the 'Islamic State' on his Instagram” account," according to the minister.

Dacic said the assailant shouted "Allahu Akbar," or "God is great" in Arabic, during the attack on the guard. According to Dacic, the guard killed the attacker in self-defense.

He said police were treating the incident as a terrorist attack, with the terrorism threat level raised to its highest, or "red alert."

"This means tighter security checks and an increased police presence at sensitive sites, including infrastructure facilities and places where large crowds gather," he said.

The attack came  just days after key early parliamentary election in Serbia and one day after Israel held its parliamentary vote, with no clear result yet in sight.

In June 2024, an attacker with a crossbow seriously wounded a Serbian police officer guarding the same embassy in Belgrade before being shot and killed by police.

That attacker was identified as a 25-year-old Islamic convert from a village near the capital who had become radicalized.

#816. Harborough sign 6ft 9in striker Hudlin before FA Cup tie

At 6ft 9in (2.06m), Hudlin is one of the tallest outfield players in the world

Non-league Harborough Town have signed striker Kyle Hudlin, one of the world's tallest professional footballers.

The 26-year-old, who is 6ft 9ins (2.06m), will be available for the National League North side's FA Cup first-round tie at League One club Leyton Orient on Saturday.

Hudlin, whose former clubs include Solihull Moors, Huddersfield Town and Newport County, most recently played for Nam Dinh in Vietnam's top flight.

"His attributes will give us more firepower going forward," Harborough boss Mitch Austin told the club website., external "I'm delighted to welcome him to the club."

Birmingham-born Hudlin scored 17 goals in 69 appearances for Solihull, including the opener in the 2022 National League play-off final.

He moved to Huddersfield that summer, gaining experience in the Championship, and spent time on loan at AFC Wimbledon, Burton Albion and Newport before leaving the Terriers in July 2025.

Austin said: "I remember watching Kyle score for Solihull in the promotion final at the London Stadium and have kept an eye on his career ever since.

"We met a few months ago through a mutual friend and, when I found out he was a free agent, I was naturally interested. What stood out first was Kyle as a person, before we even got to talking about him as a player."

Hudlin is the latest player with EFL experience to join the Bees in recent months, following the recruitment of ex-Wigan Athletic winger Michael Jacobs and former Middlesbrough and Nottingham Forest striker Britt Assombalonga.

The Leicestershire-based club last reached this stage of the FA Cup in 2024-25, before they were beaten by Reading in the second round.

Hudlin made his professional breakthrough at Solihull Moors, before moving to Huddersfield in 2022

#814. Matthias Jaissle caught in the storm as Newcastle struggle without European fix

Panic building among fans as club visit Craven Cottage but head coach has resolute support of hierarchy

At least Matthias Jaissle has a sense of humour. “There’s a lot of storm at the moment,” reflected Newcastle’s head coach on Thursday. A wry smile suggested he was not referring to the north-east weather. Jaissle has seen his tactics, team selection, man management and entire philosophy rubbished in recent days but, on current evidence, appears to be holding his nerve. After all, it is not Jaissle’s fault that his appointment has coincided with supporters, players and directors struggling to adjust to life without Champions League involvement.

A disappointing 12th-place finish under Eddie Howe last season dictates that there are no more exciting trips to Barcelona, Paris and Marseille and, significantly, no much-needed boost to club finances. Indeed, Newcastle are finding life without last term’s continental fix so tricky that they travel to Fulham on Saturday with the disgruntled mindset of a passenger accustomed to flying business class who suddenly finds themselves stuck in a cramped, mid-row economy seat.

Even worse, many fans regard the trip to Craven Cottage as a full-blown relegation six-pointer. Given Newcastle are 13th on 11 points that, ostensibly, is somewhat hysterical. Yet anyone who has watched the bulk of Newcastle’s games this season will understand the reasons underpinning the sense of panic. And if Jaissle bears some responsibility for a run of four defeats in the past five games in all competitions, Newcastle’s unwanted club record-breaking run of 14 home league matches without a clean sheet stretches back into last season.

While Jaissle’s bloody-mindedness in persisting with a 4-2-3-1 formation when he lacks both a natural No 10 and pace and mobility in central midfield merits scrutiny, he was not responsible for close-season recruitment. Ross Wilson, the sporting director, signed eight players all aged 24 or under for a combined £262.9m. Only three – Amar Dedic, Nico González and Lukas Hornicek – are likely starters at present. A fourth, Sean Steur, an 18-year-old acquired from Ajax looks potentially top-drawer but Jaissle refuses to overplay him and risk attendant physical overload.

Fingers are duly being pointed at Wilson but the need to comply with football’s spending rules explains why Newcastle sold their three best players – Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimarães – last summer. The resultant vacuum left Wilson taking calculated gambles on inexperienced youngsters, including Matias Fernandez-Pardo, a £51m forward signed from Lille, Bazoumana Touré, a £42m winger signed from Hoffenheim, and Aladji Bamba, a £30m midfielder from Monaco. Newcastle’s Saudi Arabian owners hope they will prove unpolished gems with high resale values, but only one of those eight new faces, González, possesses Premier League experience. Throw in a youthful, relatively inexperienced manager and the risk is obvious.

While football’s financial regulations have triggered such wholesale player trading at a moment when Newcastle’s commercial revenues fail to match their ambitions, it did not help that Howe hoarded first-teamers, consistently resisting the opportunity to sell stars at peak value. Indeed, Alexander Isak only joined Liverpool for £125m last year after going on strike. The absence of a sporting director at that time left Howe and his nephew, Andy Howe, then a senior Newcastle recruitment executive, heavily involved in reinvesting the cash. The best part of £225m was poured into signing Nick Woltemade, Yoane Wissa, Anthony Elanga and Jacob Ramsey, but that quartet have collectively underwhelmed.

When a disillusioned, burned-out Howe quit three weeks before the new season, Wilson and Newcastle’s chief executive, David Hopkinson, had already lined up his successor. Jaissle’s much-vaunted attacking brand of so-called vertical football had secured two Asian Champions Leagues at Al-Ahli. On Tyneside, though, such ‘verticality’ has frequently turned into a series of optimistic long balls punctuating matches that frequently see Newcastle’s midfield overrun, forwards isolated and defenders exposed. Given that possession retention has long been a problem for a team arguably at their best when choreographed in contain-and-counter mode, Jaissle’s blueprint appears overly ambitious.

Newcastle’s formidable attacking pace menaces on the break but the manager’s plan during the 1-0 home defeat against Everton last Monday was to bisect the visiting lines courtesy of sharp incisive passing along the ground. It did not work and afterwards Jaissle criticised his players for disobeying orders, insisting “shooting long balls” had never been on the agenda. “It was not the plan and that is something you need to clearly mention,” he told reporters.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

By Thursday Jaissle looked considerably happier, insisting there was no discord between management and players. “Everyone believes in the long-term project,” he said. Jaissle had apparently been encouraged by his shot-shy players’ willingness to sign up for extra shooting practice but perhaps Dedic took such instruction too literally. On Wednesday afternoon, the Bosnia international sparked the involvement of an armed response unit after being spotted with a bow and arrow in the Northumberland countryside. The police swiftly accepted that the equipment was for “recreational use” but what has been described as a “naive misunderstanding” seems horribly emblematic of Newcastle’s season.

One thing remains clear: after describing Jaissle as “fire” and a “rock star” – not to mention paying Al-Ahli £9.5m to release him – Hopkinson will not sack the 38-year-old German lightly. He and Wilson are standing resolutely by their man.

“Everyone’s aware of, and realistic, about the journey ahead and where we are right now,” said Jaissle. “The nice part is that I get even more the feeling from the club of how committed they are.”

#813. Wolves legend and ex-England defender Coady retires

Conor Coady made 317 of his 503 club appearances in a Wolves shirt

Wolverhampton Wanderers legend Conor Coady has retired from playing at the age of 33.

The former Wolves skipper, who won 10 England caps as a central defender, has been linked with a move into coaching at club level, having already taken up an opening with England Under-21s, external under Lee Carsley on 4 September.

Coady had also been helping out within his first club Liverpool's Under-21 set-up, prior to his deadline day departure from Wrexham.

It was at Liverpool where it all began for Coady as a promising midfielder in the academy at Kirkby, where his tall, angular build and highly promising form for the reserve team evoked obvious comparisons in some quarters to fellow Liverpudlian Steven Gerrard.

Coady had made just two first-team appearances when he moved on from Anfield, first on loan to Sheffield United in 2013, before signing for Huddersfield Town at the end of that season.

But he enjoyed most of his success at Molineux after being converted into a central defender by then Wolves boss Nuno Espirito Santo.

He also played for Everton, Leicester City, Wrexham and then on loan at Charlton Athletic last season in his 503-game eight-club career.

Coady was first signed for Wolves by Kenny Jackett in 2015 - and played a major part in the club's promotion back to the Premier League in 2018.

He captained the Wolves team who twice finished seventh and also reached the quarter-finals of the Europa League.

In all, he made 317 Wolves appearances, scoring seven of his career tally - for club and country - of 22 goals, before being allowed to leave on loan for Everton in 2022.

He then joined Leicester for a reported Â£8.5m in July 2023 after Everton opted not to complete a Â£4.5m deal to turn his season-long loan into a permanent switch.

Coady then moved on for 13 months on the books at Wrexham, which was ended prematurely before his final loan move to The Valley, to join Nathan Jones' Charlton.

But he had not figured this season prior to his official exit from the Racecourse Ground.

Having worked regularly as a pundit for BBC Radio 5 Live to hint at a future media career, Coady has already been linked with the role of assistant head coach at League One side Barnsley.

#812. Rise of the ‘schooligans’: how a wave of antisocial behaviour threatens non-league football

Teenage ultras are increasingly causing disorder and communities fear it will not be long before it becomes something more dangerous

It is five past three on Saturday afternoon and the teenage ultras of Hednesford Town are running late. They have arrived in Chester for their team’s National League North fixture and have hailed taxis, determined to make their presence felt at the ground. But word appears to have got out about their arrival. As one car turns away from the city’s charming half-timbered houses and into narrow residential streets, half a dozen local youths appear, haring round the corner in balaclavas. They try to attack the cab and chase after it as it pulls away. The smell of pyro is everywhere. As the taxi finally gets clear, the Chester gang stops in the middle of the road, shouting and gesticulating. One lad, no older than 16, pulls a long blade from inside his trousers and brandishes it.

The incident ended there and no one was hurt, though a police investigation has been launched. The match went off without trouble too and the Hednesford gang – known at home as the “schooligans” – were escorted safely back to the station by Cheshire police. It was just another weekend in English non-league football, where a wave of antisocial behaviour is causing concern and leading the UK Football Policing Unit (UKFPU) to declare it its “most important” priority. As the disorder continues, a question remains: how long will it be before teenage trouble-making becomes something more dangerous?

This year clubs from the south coast to the north-east have reported disorder caused by supporters under the age of 18, some seemingly as young as 10. In February, Aldershot Town experienced a series of disorderly incidents involving young people that included brawls outside the ground, behaviour the club described as “wholly unacceptable and [which] will not be tolerated”. In August, Enfield Town said they were “concerned and disappointed” by young fans at a fixture in Lewes. Two weeks ago, a Gloucester City fan was hit by a rock thrown by teenagers at Redditch United during an FA Trophy tie. Even Soham Town Rangers of the ninth-tier Eastern Counties League urged parents to ensure their children make “sensible choices” ahead of a match against Mildenhall Town.

Hednesford have experienced consistent trouble for a number of seasons and in August their owner and chair, Craig Gwilt, attempted to face it down. A rising tide of disorder was harming the club, he said, behaviour that included “pitch invasions, fighting, abuse directed towards players, missiles being thrown at opposition goalkeepers, flares entering the field of play and even interference with players’ water bottles”. He called on fans to improve their behaviour or risk permanently damaging the club. The plea was not immediately heard. Three weeks after Gwilt’s statement the club banned 20 young supporters from attending matches after there was action away at Telford.

Hednesford is a town of 19,000 people on the edge of the protected landscape of Cannock Chase. The town centre is neat and tidy, a well-maintained monument to the Stafford regiment at its heart. On the way to the ground you can get a pint at the Cross Keys where Dick Turpin reputedly rested his head. It’s a town seemingly at peace with itself and the club is at the heart of the community. But both are struggling to get to grips with an issue that leaves people scratching their heads.

This season the club have introduced measures to prevent under-16s from entering without an accompanying adult. There is also extra security on matchdays, ostensibly to manage car parking. These interventions appear to have contained any trouble in and around the stadium, but now gangs of up to 50 youths will gather post-match at a safe remove to look for trouble or, more likely, save their energy for an away fixture. Like the one at Chester, for example, when the schooligans were removed from one train for antisocial behaviour and were drinking alcohol throughout their journey up. Encountering such groups on a Saturday will be familiar to many rail passengers.

The schooligans, whose nickname was coined by Hednesford’s security staff, “baffle” the club’s chief executive, Marvin Robinson, who would rather be spending his time modernising a club that have had back-to-back promotions. “I’m not really sure I understand why it seems to be a trend,” he says. “It’s a wider social issue but what is it and what will it become? Is it a social media thing? Is it about notoriety or becoming known for something? The adult response online has been almost to normalise it. I don’t agree with that.”

Go on TikTok and the picture does start to become a little clearer. From aggregator accounts to individual semi-anonymised accounts belonging to the teenagers, there is a wealth of posts celebrating the behaviour of “top lads” who “mooch” to the ground before “running” the opposition out of town. Often set to a backing of euphoric electronic dance music with a layer or two of visual effects and captions such as “this weekend’s got me feeling like a little kid at Christmas”, the posts are celebratory and almost nostalgic in tone. In recent weeks TikTok has begun appending disclaimers to them that read: “Participating in this activity could result in you or others getting hurt.” TikTok removed an account named “NLN [National League North] gimps and chants”, when alerted to it by the Guardian, for contravening guidelines that do not allow content that glorifies violence.

The mythology of old-school football hooliganism appears to be well‑known among these groups, with references to the 2005 film Green Street commonplace. But the schooligans of 2026 don’t behave like the firms of the past. For a start they rarely, if at all, arrange to fight their rivals. Instead they use the mapping feature on Snapchat to alert opposition to their presence on the day, and take it from there. The concept of rivalry itself is fluid. In the West Midlands, for example, teens from Hednesford will band together with those nominally affiliated with Redditch or Cannock Town. When there was trouble recently at Hednesford’s fixture at Hereford, local police said the majority of disorder had been caused by Redditch fans chasing supporters from Solihull Moors. It isn’t just local either. Children as young as 12 have been detained in the north-west having travelled from the south coast, a distance of more than 200 miles.

The chair of Redditch, David Faulkner, is still dealing with the fallout from the Gloucester tie two weeks ago. He says the fluid set of alliances between ultra groups has created a “travelling circus” and that no one knows where it will turn up next. Branding himself “the non-League chair”, Faulkner has started posting videos on YouTube drawing attention to the disorder and calling for collective action.

“People think of non-league football as one man and his dog, but we need to catch up with the fact that it’s massive now,” Faulkner says. “Some clubs have attendances bigger than in League One but the regulations were put in place decades ago. We need that extra regulation, that support, so we can get the funding to put things like CCTV and more stewarding in place. Because the other way this could go is that [change only happens] when someone gets seriously hurt. I haven’t got metal detectors on our gates to stop kids bringing knives in. None of that stuff. I’d rather take action before something happens.”

The Football Association says the behaviour of fans is primarily a matter for clubs and relevant authorities but that it is working to develop policies that welcome young fans safely to National League grounds. The UK Football Policing Unit, meanwhile, is working alongside leagues and the Crown Prosecution Service to develop new policies around “youth risk”, which are likely to include an extra focus on education via schools and community work.

“It’s probably the most important area of football policing that we’re focused on,” says Mike Ankers, the deputy director of the UKFPU. “We are seeing children as young as 12 or 13 engaged in antisocial behaviour at best, but also actual violence and that’s up and down the country, with some travelling hundreds of miles. There comes a great risk and a great safeguarding issue with regards to that. In terms of our focus, we are making sure that we bring the right people together to have a solution. It’s not just the policing, it requires a more holistic view.”

Ankers says he supports Faulkner in speaking up on the topic and believes many more adults need to take responsibility. “These children need a strong adult role model,” he says. “I would very much question that if your 12-year-old is going out to follow football and is being detained, perhaps 200 miles away, then you need to look at how they’ve been able to travel and have those conversations. I think there’s very much a role for parental responsibility.”

The Hednesford schooligans, having been deposited on the platform at Chester by police, made their way home by train, only to find themselves stuck in a combination of Halloween revellers and national signal failure. Constrained, they hunched over their phones viewing footage from different teenage firms and discussed the day’s events. In the end, they concurred they had got the best of it. After all, said one: “What experience do you get from chasing a taxi?”

TikTok and Snapchat were approached for comment.

#811. Hailee Steinfeld Reveals What She Didn’t Expect From Motherhood

Hailee Steinfeld detailed what she’s learned about herself from the “transformative experience” of being a mom to her and Josh Allen’s baby girl Harper.

Hailee Steinfeld is learning to play new notes as a first-time mom.

Six months after she gave birth to baby girl Harper with husband Josh Allen, the Pitch Perfect 2 star shed light on the unexpected impact motherhood has had on her relationship with herself.

“There’s a long answer, but I’ll give the short one here: I’ve learned just how much of myself I still have to discover,” Steinfeld wrote the Nov. 3 edition of her Beau Society newsletter on Substack, in response to a fan question. “I thought becoming a mom would be this transformative experience about loving someone else, and it is that 1000 percent.”

“But what I didn’t expect is how much she’s teaching me about myself,” she added. “She’s made me more patient, more present, and so much more aware of how special the little things are.”

And as the Hexed actress continues to discover new aspects about herself amid her motherhood journey, she’s also learning to take her own advice.

“I’m really good at reminding people that they’re human, that things take time, and that everything happens for a reason,” Steinfeld wrote, “and it will all fall into place—how, when, and where it should—and that they don’t have to have everything all figured out.”

Yet, she admitted, “I’m not always the best at taking that advice myself.”

But since becoming a mom, the Sinners star—who married Allen in May 2025—has made sure that her own wellbeing is still a priority.

“This season of life has definitely taught me to slow down, really just soak in the small pockets of joy that are truly all around us,” she shared on the Nov. 5 episode of Live With Kelly and Mark. “Time for myself looks a little different now, but I find it.”

And this mindset of cherishing every moment is surely beneficial when it comes to wrapping her heard around how fast her daughter is growing up.

“I feel like she’s 6 months, and also 4 weeks, and also 5 years old,” Steinfeld told Kelly Ripa and Mark Consuelos. “Time is crazy how it works.”

“She is totally on the move,” she added. “This girl is crawling around.”
