#810. Africa's first Youth Olympics open in Senegal amid hope and scrutiny

Senegal is hosting Africa's first Youth Olympics, with 2,700 young athletes competing in Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly. The Games bring pride and hope, but also questions over cost, rights and legacy.

On the final day of October, what may well be the final Summer Youth Olympics ever will begin. It will be the first on African soil as around 2,700 athletes aged 15-17 arrive in Senegal to compete across a total of 153 events in 25 sports.

Hosted in eight venues across three locations – Dakar, Diamniadio and Saly, 80 kilometers (50 miles) from the capital – these Games are seen by many as a prelude to Africa hosting a full Olympics one day in the future.

"I'm really excited about the Youth Olympic Games because, for the first time, I'll be representing our country," 15-year-old judoka Aisha Diop who is competing for Senegal told DW.

"I am very proud to be able to represent my country at these Games. This will really motivate young African athletes because they will improve, and they will want to continue playing sports now that the Youth Games have been held here."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The 2026 Youth Games in Senegal will also be a first beyond the history it is making in Africa.

"Of the 2,700 athletes who will be competing in Dakar, there will be a 50-50 split between men and women," Olivia Nloga, Chief Brand Promotion Officer on the organizing committee, told DW.

"But this parity isn't just reflected in the overall figure. This gender parity will also be reflected in each event and in each sport where such parity actually exists."

Several sports are also making their debut at the Youth Olympic Games, such as five-a-side baseball, kung fu and the Senegalese specialty of beach wrestling. There's also a refugee team at the Youth Olympic Games for the first time.

"As I said earlier, the Youth Olympic Games aren't just about sports, and they aren't just about infrastructure," said Nloga.

"For us, it was also important to use this time to build on and reinforce the idea that these Games in Senegal are a celebration for the people. We did this by investing in culture—for example, through a fashion show and a program called Yi-sol, which is a mural project on the city's walls."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Other projects designed to celebrate the people include music, and a local student designed the mascot. The biggest focus of all though, is on creating sustainability for the young people of Senegal.

"We did so through a program that is very important to us – one that is close to our hearts, namely, the Olympic Civic and Sports Certificate," Nloga said.

"We traveled to schools throughout Senegal and worked with more than 1,000 instructors to reach and make an impact on more than one million young Senegalese children who, during this hiatus, were exposed to and educated about the values of the Olympic Movement."

With recent flooding in the country, there were concerns that infrastructure would have been affected, but Nloga insisted that flood risk had long been in the planning.

"The prime minister held an interdepartmental meeting during which he established a task force to ensure that the necessary arrangements and follow-up measures are put in place to safeguard both the competition venues and the accommodation sites."

With Formula 1 confirming its return to Africa earlier in October, global sport is slowly becoming a more regular event in Africa. As a result though, there have been questions asked about the legacy of such events.

Many in Senegal concerned by the high cost of living and unemployment will see these Games as an unnecessary expense. For the Senegalese authorities though, they are an opportunity for long-term investment in the country's young people as well as infrastructure. There is also the hope that this will make Dakar a major tourist destination.

There was further criticism of the Games being in Senegal from Human Rights Watch (HRW), with the NGO calling on the Senegalese authorities to change their stance on the LGBTQ+ community.

"You are welcoming all of the world. It shouldn't be 'you are welcome to our country, except this, except that,'" Larissa Kojoue from HRW told DW.

"Anti-LGBT legislation and that crackdown that is going on, they contradict the Olympic movement, the Olympic Charter, and also various human rights convention that the country has signed."

Earlier this year, Senegal President Bassirou Diomaye Faye signed into law new legislation on same-sex relations that have proved contentious abroad despite broad political support within the majority Muslim country's parliament. Several human rights groups had voiced concerns about the bill, including warning that it would dissuade people at risk of illnesses like HIV/AIDS from seeking help.

The Games were set to see the return of Russians to Olympic competition under their own colours after the International Olympic Committee (IOC) lifted their suspension in July.

However, the Russian Athletics Federation (RusAF) released a statement the day before the opening ceremony saying the reported 13 athletes (and 10 coaches) had been exluded from the competition. They demanded an explanation and asked for the decision to be reconsidered.

"The IOC-endorsed position was clear in its direction: young athletes holding Russian or Belarusian passports should no longer be restricted from international youth competitions. That principle should apply to Dakar 2026," read the statement.

Despite the IOC's ruling, each federation can still decide whether to authorize Russian participation. World Athletics, has clearly upheld their ban, while swimming and judo have allowed Russian athletes back.

"This has enabled World Athletics to pursue its own exclusory agenda in the face of clear and just directions from the IOC. This activism is only detrimental to youth sports, with the result being that Russian young athletes will be denied the opportunity to compete at these Games."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Despite the various concerns, there is an overriding hope that the Games will be prove beneficial for all involved.

"What makes the Youth Olympic Games in Dakar special is that they are also rooted in Senegal's extremely strong sporting culture," Nloga said.

"Every evening, when you take a stroll along the Corniche in Dakar, you're struck by the number of people you see exercising, regardless of their age or physical condition. What we'll be offering during these Olympic Games is also an immersion into Senegalese life – into the way sports are just as much a part of Senegalese identity."

This article was updated on October 30, 2026 to reflect the change in situation for Russian athletes at the Games.

Sira Thierij conducted interviews for this article. Edited by: Chuck Penfold

#809. Palmer misses too many chances to impress - Tuchel

Thomas Tuchel has named three uncapped players in his England squad

England manager Thomas Tuchel said Cole Palmer "misses too many chances to impress" after not selecting the Chelsea forward for November's Nations League fixtures.

Palmer, 24, dropped out of England's squad for their previous games in early autumn and is absent again for matches against Croatia at Wembley on Thursday, 12 November and Spain in Madrid on Sunday, 15 November.

Tuchel has instead handed Fulham's Josh King and Borussia Dortmund's Jobe Bellingham their first England call-ups. Both players are attacking midfielders.

"We have enough number 10s and we stick to the guys who were in the previous camp because we were happy with the two and a half weeks we had together," said Tuchel.

"We have Josh King as a new player in there, but I want to see him on both wings. He is kind of an extra player and he can play all four positions.

"I guess everyone is desperate to play for England and Cole is no exception.

"We are speaking now about a player that is not in camp. It counts when you are in camp and I just said last time that he misses too many opportunities to impress."

Jobe, 21, joins his brother Jude in the England squad - and they could be the first pair of siblings to feature in an England line-up since Gary and Phil Neville.

England sit second behind Spain in group A3 of the Nations League with three wins and a loss.

One more point from their remaining two matches will secure a place in the two-legged quarter-finals in March, with the winners of those ties advancing to the Nations League Finals in June.

'Palmer misses too many opportunities to impress' - Tuchel

Catch-up with all Thomas Tuchel's responses at his squad selection news conference

Goalkeepers: Jordan Pickford (Everton), Jason Steele (Brighton & Hove Albion), James Trafford (Leeds United)

Defenders: Trent Alexander-Arnold (Real Madrid), Jarrad Branthwaite (Everton), Marc Guehi (Manchester City), Lewis Hall (Newcastle United), Ezri Konsa (Arsenal), Jarell Quansah (Bayer Leverkusen), Djed Spence (Inter Milan), Ben White (Arsenal)

Forwards: Dominic Calvert-Lewin (Leeds United), Eberechi Eze (Arsenal), Morgan Gibbs-White (Nottingham Forest), Anthony Gordon (Barcelona), Harry Kane (Bayern Munich), Rio Ngumoha (Liverpool), Morgan Rogers (Chelsea)

The selection of Jobe Bellingham for the senior squad means he continues to follow in the footsteps of his older brother.

Both graduates of the Birmingham City academy, the brothers were regular selections in England youth line-ups.

Jobe joined Dortmund from Sunderland in summer 2025 in a deal worth up to Â£31m, having helped the Wearside club win promotion to the Premier League via the play-offs.

The move mirrored one made by Jude, 23, who played for the German side between 2020 and 2023 before signing for Real Madrid.

Tuchel said England Under-21 coach Lee Carsley had been "speaking very highly" of Jobe Bellingham "for a while".

"He is the captain of the under-21s so I think the door should always be open and the pathway should always be open for special performances over a long period of time and that is what Jobe has done," he added.

"He found his way and his rhythm with Dortmund, where he has had an excellent start to the season. He is a regular starter there and now very influential."

Bellingham has been preferred to Kobbie Mainoo, with Tuchel saying the Manchester United midfielder, who was an early withdrawal from the last squad, has had a "difficult spell with his club".

"The door is always open for younger players to overtake and make their mark," he added.

King has had a strong start to the Premier League season, scoring two goals and making one assist, and has played at every youth level for England.

The 19-year-old Fulham academy graduate has scored one goal in nine appearances for England Under-21s, and Tuchel called him "a fantastic character" who "gives us a bit of flexibility".

"We decided to nominate 22 outfield players for flexibility in training and he is the extra player in training, if you will," Tuchel added.

Alonso praises Palmer's quality and attitude

Arsenal forward Bukayo Saka misses out on the November fixtures after sustaining a quadriceps injury against Bayern Munich last month.

The Premier League champions believe the 25-year-old will be absent for six weeks after he was substituted early in the Champions League game against Bayern Munich.

Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott is also not selected after picking up an injury against Croatia in October.

The 23-year-old, who made his England debut in the first international break of the season and was described as "the complete package" by Tuchel, is reportedly in contention to return for the Cherries against Ipswich on Sunday.

Manchester United's Marcus Rashford and Newcastle's Tino Livramento, who both pulled out the last squad prior to any matches being played, also miss out with respective hip and knee injuries.

Como's Trevoh Chalobah is another absentee, while Manchester City's Nico O'Reilly and Rico Lewis have also not been selected.

James Garner of Everton and Nottingham Forest's Morgan Gibbs-White retain their places after being added to England's last squad prior to any fixtures being played, while Arsenal's Ben White and Inter Milan's Djed Spence return for the first time since the summer.

The Arsenal pair of Declan Rice and Ezri Konsa, who both withdrew from the last England party, are fit and selected.

#808. Infantino caught in the web as tide turns against Trump in midterms and leaves Fifa exposed | Barney Ronay

Trump Exposed Reactor Core Syndrome very much in play after Democrat landslide – and Fifa’s president may pay a price

Oh baby, clamp me in your repulsive mouthparts. Sink your unusually large and venomous fangs into my abdomen. And yes, we are doing this in the White House cabinet rooms, out there in plain sight of the watching world, just a gleaming golden ball between us. But it’s fine. Probably. Now take a sip of those sweet, sweet tiny male arachnoid entrails.

An exciting new study was published over the summer into the habits of the Australian redback spider. The research made headlines for its focus on reproductive behaviour, specifically the male’s urgent and very willing engagement in what is known as sexual cannibalism, AKA copulatory suicide.

Scientists observing these tiny arachnoids discovered that during the act of lovemaking with the larger, more decorative female, the male will perform a spectacular sexual death-somersault, flipping himself upside down, presenting his underbelly to the female’s fangs, and urging her to literally consume his intestines mid-coitus as an energy snack and self-dooming sweetener. You’ve already ripped my heart out, babe. Now take my guts as well.

This doesn’t paint a very flattering picture of the male redback’s sense of himself, his ability to recognise boundaries in a relationship. Overall, the picture is of a craven, fawning, hairless entity, entirely in thrall to its power-master. Yes, it might make sense for a while to place your prospects in the hands of a glassy-eyed red-tinged predator at the heart of a toxic web of power. But it can land you in a spot of bother down the line.

In unrelated news, there was a sense this week that Gianni Infantino’s entanglements with Donald Trump may have now moved one step closer to scrutiny, sunlight, consequences, perhaps even some kind of decisive intestinal devouring. The sight of Infantino cavorting for the US president was one of the more grotesque sport-adjacent spectacles of recent times. What kind of relationship was this?

How will history remember that display of power-fluffing, the supposedly apolitical Fifa president sat nodding gravely at the walnut-veneered table as the latest immigration policy is trailed, beaming along as some random crypto-waffle is chucked into the mix, and becoming through this an ever more contorted figure, as though essence of human mendacity has been condensed, reconstituted into a fine paste, pumped into a serge blue suit and taught to walk around saying the phrase: “My magic ball unites the golden peace world.”

At the time it felt as though this was some kind of warning siren, a real-time satire on the idea of unaccountable executive power. Is this just allowed now, confirmation in human form that acting as though you exist outside the rules is halfway to actually being there?

Well, maybe not. As of Wednesday there is for the first time a sense of something potentially self-dooming about that public two-hander. Perhaps this is the best way to picture those interactions now, Infantino backflipped in supplication, thighs clamped around the presidential shoulders, presenting his tenderest parts to those razor-sharp mandibles. Feast on my entrails. Consume my borrowed sporting soul. Empower me. Or don’t. Whatever. We’ll talk later.

Trump may be heading into a diminished final two years in office. But Trump Exposed Reactor Core Syndrome is still very much in play, a principle that states, yes, he will give you heat, light and a deathly glow. But he will also melt your face in the process. And maybe this process is now finally coming for the world’s second-most-provocative elected president.

The headline Fifa news this week was the council member Kozo Tashima’s announcement that he will stand as a candidate in March’s leadership vote. There is, at the very least, someone else to vote for now. In the wider world, but potentially more significant to the Infantino regime, the US midterm elections brought a Democratic landslide in the Senate and the House of Representatives.

Football is, as ever, just a tiny notch on the to-do list. To date those results are simply a rejection of something, the chance to luxuriate in the defenestrating of some of those High Trump oddities, the senator who believes a cabal of Sikhs is trying to steal the moon, the House representative on record as saying all Eritreans are genetically derived from yoghurt, the one-term governor who looks as if he bites the heads off sparrows and wears a suit made entirely from recycled human fingernails.

What comes next is not clear. But there is talk of cleaning house. Internal judicial matters are now firmly in the hands of Trump’s opponents. Some Democrats have warned of the need to “lawyer up”, have spoken about correcting the most excessive acts of opportunism over the past two years.

Even as Infantino is out there bartering for his future, bothered at mosquito-level by a cloud of revelations – the use of Fifa resources to electioneer, talk of having his maid’s visa raised at government level – the one thing that may actually get close to him is force majeure.

At which point enter the tantalising figure of Jamie Raskin, representative for Maryland’s 8th district, and widely tipped to become the new chair of the House judiciary committee. Raskin is a hawk on what he describes as “the corruption” of aspects of the Trump regime. And these include Fifa.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Raskin’s letter to Infantino dated 26 July bears re-reading. First he brings up the wire fraud and money laundering case against Full Play Group that was part of the 2015 indictments against the Blatter regime and that was dropped by the Trump administration because it was “not a priority”.

He refers to “Fifa’s brazen campaign to curry favour with Donald Trump since his re-election”, the “hilariously fake ‘Fifa Peace Prize’”, the leasing of office space in Trump Tower at an economically irrational rate, describing this and other elements as a “strategy of outright bribery”.

Examples of price gouging and “fraudulent sales tactics” are mentioned as a lever for a potentially fascinating disclosure of Fifa communications with the Trump organisation, and the promise of a full congressional investigation.

This was sabre-rattling at the time. It isn’t any more. The letter was also sent before the Joshua Kushner-linked scheme to sell off part of the World Cup to private equity, described by Raskin as a “smash-and-grab scam of colossal proportions”. “Now we see where all the bribes, kickbacks and sweetheart deals have been leading,” he told the Guardian. Are you excited yet? Does this sound like possible fangs of doom stuff?

This is the same Democrat who could now have the authority to compel testimony and documents from Fifa, JP Morgan – the bank involved in the sell-off process – and entities associated with the Kushner family. The Trump White House has in the past dismissed such allegations as politically motivated. Fifa has kept its head down. Well, good luck with that now.

Who knows? Even the noise, the heat and the potential ripples may be enough for some of those being asked to vote in Rabat next year. Infantino’s self-promotion as a one-man global brand, the royal court persona, the selfie with Pelé’s coffin, the micromanaging of the vote for Saudi 2034. All this creates its own internal tensions.

There would of course be satisfaction at witnessing a redback-style ending. Even if, as ever, the worst part is the feeling of sadness, of chances missed, the thought of what could have been done with all this power in larger, less grasping, less mandible-like hands.

The wheels of justice can be disappointingly clogged and reluctant to grind. But this feels motivated and public enough to carry some energy. There is at least a ball rolling now. Plus the central irony, that Infantino made himself a player here, dared the world to watch, and willingly hurled himself into that cannibalistic embrace.

#807. JonBenét Ramsey's Brother Burke Shares "Best Chance" at Solving Murder

JonBenét Ramsey's brother Burke Ramsey shared in a rare interview how DNA evidence found on her underwear and underneath her fingernails is the "best chance" at solving her murder 30 years later.

JonBenét Ramsey's brother has not given up on the search for her killer nearly three decades later.

Breaking his 10-year public silence, Burke Ramsey detailed his belief that DNA belonging to an "unknown male intruder" found on his slain sister's underwear and beneath her finger may be "the best evidence we have."

"We need to find that match," he told the Daily Mail in an interview published Nov. 5. "It's probably the person who did it, you know, and it's the best chance we have to solve this."

"And I want it solved," the 39-year-old continued. "I don't know much about the scientific nitty-gritty and it's hard to learn the details of the case, because it is emotionally taxing. But they need to send those samples to different labs again and keep testing."

He added, "Find the match. That will go a long way to bringing justice."

Burke was 9 years old when his sister JonBenét, 6, was reported missing from their family’s Colorado home on Dec. 26, 1996. Her body was eventually found in the basement, with her cause of death ruled as asphyxia by strangulation and blunt head trauma.

In 2003, Burke and his parents, John Bennett Ramsey and the late Patsy Ramsey, were ruled out as contributors to the unknown DNA discovered on JonBenét. And though Burke in particular has been the subject of many online theories, he and the Ramsay family has long denied his involvement in his sister’s death.

Aside from DNA evidence, which John alleged in 2024 hadn’t been tested, investigators through the years have also homed in on a handwritten ransom note for $118,000 found in the Ramseys' family home on the day of JonBenét disappearance.

For John, now 82, he believes the note is an important clue to his daughter's unsolved murder.

"One of the theories that I came up with," he shared in a 20/20 in unearthed in 2024, "that it was close to the net amount I'd received that year as a bonus."

John surmised that the number "means something" to the murderer.

"Whether that's tied to my bonus or something else, we don't know," he added. "Only the killer knows."

In the decades since her shocking death, the unsolved JonBenét case has continued to be the subject of public fascination. For more inside the tragedy and its long aftermath, keep reading…

After Patsy Ramsey called 911 at 5:52 a.m. on Dec. 26, 1996, to report that her daughter JonBenét Ramsey had been kidnapped, she and husband John Ramsey also reached out to a number of their friends, who came right over to support the couple.

In turn, in addition to responding officers, there were people milling around the Ramseys' 5,000-square-foot home all day before John found JonBenét's body in the basement shortly after 1:30 p.m.

"I should have removed all those people from the scene, that was a crime scene mistake," retired Boulder Police Detective Bob Whitson recalled in the Netflix docuseries Cold Case: Who Killed JonBenét Ramsey. "But, at the time, it looked like a legitimate kidnapping. So, I thought, Well, these are the support system for the Ramseys, and I let 'em stay."

Not knowing she was dead when he found her, John said in the series he at first tried to untie the cord that bound her hands. The knots were too tight, he said, but he did remove a piece of duct tape that was covering her mouth and tossed it onto a blanket that had been with the body.

He then carried her upstairs, which, according to investigators, ensured that the evidence collected from her body, the pajamas she was wearing, the tape, etc., was contaminated.

"There may have been some evidence on the duct tape if that wasn't removed," Whitson said in the series.

Police who responded to Patsy's 911 call searched the three upper levels of the Ramseys' home, and the basement, but it wasn't until a detective suggested that John do another sweep of the house nearly eight hours later that her body was found in a part of the basement that used to be a coal room.

"One of the cops did not open the door where JonBenét was lying," Fox News' Carol McKinley, who covered the case at the time, said in the Netflix series. "Major mistake, and I believe he lives with that to this day."

Retired Boulder PD Commander John San Agustin noted in the series, "You never have someone outside of law enforcement doing a search."

However, when John looked in the coal room, he said, "Her body was right there in front of me."

In a pre-Toddlers and Tiaras world, the media incredulously spotlighted JonBenét's participation in children's beauty pageants, with most of the commentary being of the what-sort-of-mother-lets-her-child-parade-around-like-that variety.

Having competed and performed at local events since she was 4, there were myriad photos of JonBenét wearing a full face of makeup and videos that became Rorschach tests for critics of the Ramseys who were looking for signs of sexual abuse or other trauma behind the child's precocious poise.

And people who claimed to have diagnosed as much had no qualms saying it on TV, the Netflix series including a clip from Geraldo in which a woman identified as a "well-known expert in child abuse" described one of JonBenét's performances as masturbatory. (Host Geraldo Rivera was staging a mock trial on his show, during which a six-person "jury" found Patsy liable for her daughter's death. "I went to bed for about two days," she said in the 1998 documentary The Ramseys vs. The Media, "because I just was mortified.")

Reflecting on his enthusiastic coverage of the case, Rivera told the Chicago Tribune in 2006, "Everyone I came in contact with was talking about the Ramsey case, whether it was my nanny or the people in the neighborhood or the guy that takes care of my koi pond." Even his mom wanted the details, he added, so "when it gets to that level, you know it has an interest that’s almost universal."

The pageant commentary painted the Ramseys as "delinquent parents," recalled Paula Woodward, an investigative reporter for KUSA Denver who covered the case from the beginning.

She interviewed JonBenét's pediatrician at the time, the journalist said, "He told me, no, she's never had any sexual abuse in her life. He would have lost his medical license if he ever lied about that."

In a 1997 interview, the doctor said there was "never any hint whatsoever of sexual abuse. I didn't see any hint of emotional abuse, or physical abuse. She was a very much-loved child."

But, as seen on tabloid covers shown in the series, there was plenty of speculation that the child may have been abused in lieu of evidence to allege that she really was.

"Let me address it very directly: I did not kill my daughter JonBenét," John told reporters during a May 1, 1997, news conference. "There have been innuendos that she had been or was sexually molested. I can tell you that those were the most hurtful innuendos to us as a family. They are totally false. JonBenét and I had a very close relationship. I will miss her dearly the rest of my life."

Added Patsy, "I'm appalled that anyone would think that John or I would be involved in such a hideous, heinous crime. But let me assure you that I did not kill JonBenét and did not have anything to do with it. I loved that child with the whole of my heart and soul."

JonBenét was laid to rest in Atlanta next to her half-sister Beth Ramsey (one of John's three grown children from his first marriage, she died in a car accident in 1992) on Dec. 31, 1996.

By then, the family had a spokesperson releasing statements to the media and had hired a lawyer.

Which, at the time, "smelled a little funny," Fox News' McKinley said in the series. "And we were like, 'What is going on?'"

John said in the series, however, that their attorneys had advised them to be careful about anything they said or did. "But we gave the police everything they asked for," John said. "Blood samples, DNA samples, whatever they asked for. Records, all our credit card [records], anything they asked for, we gave it to them."

Meanwhile, he added, "I would've been happy to die, quite frankly, to relieve the pain."

But with the media filling in the blanks so long as the Ramseys remained silent, soon enough friends in Boulder advised them to grant an interview ASAP, John recalled. So he and Patsy sat down with CNN on Jan. 1, 1997.

"There is a killer on the loose," Patsy memorably said at the time. "I don't know who it is, I don't know if it's a he or a she. But if I were a resident of Boulder, I would tell my friends to keep your babies close to you. There's someone out there."

Following the Ramseys' interview, then-Boulder Mayor Leslie Durgin said on TV that there was no visible sign of forced entry at the Ramsey residence and the cops were saying, based on where JonBenét's body was found, that "someone had to know the house. So, there isn't a crazed killer on the loose wandering the streets of Boulder."

Listening to Durgin, "You would assume that she had information from the police that led her to feel comfortable saying that," recalled KMGH Denver investigative reporter Julie Hayden in the Netflix series, explaining why authorities' behavior in those early days also contributed to the cloud of suspicion growing around John and Patsy. The "implication from that clearly would be that it was somebody connected with the family."

Accusations That the Ramseys' Grieving Was Staged

Journalist McKinley recalled in the series thinking that the Ramseys made "an orchestrated appearance" at a Jan. 5, 1997, memorial for their daughter in Boulder. "It didn't seem sincere to me and it was almost like a performance," she added, singling out Patsy's big black sunglasses and all-black attire as a particularly notable touch.

John barely remembered that day "'cause we were in shock, frankly," he said in the series, but any accusation that aspects of it were staged was "absolutely false."

Local media were getting a lot of information from law enforcement sources, often crediting just one source if that's all they could get, several journalists noted in the series. And not all of it was factual.

Charlie Brennan of the Rocky Mountain News admitted getting it wrong when he reported for the paper that John, a licensed pilot, had flown JonBenét's coffin to Atlanta in his own plane.

"That was inaccurate," he said in the Netflix series. "It came from a source that I thoroughly trusted and had given me other solid information. That information was wrong, my source was wrong in that case, and that was a mistake."

The Colorado Bureau of Investigation's report stating that unidentified male DNA found on JonBenét's underwear and under her fingernails did not match her father or her then-10-year-old brother Burke Ramsey came back on Jan. 15, 1997. But police didn't share the findings right away—not even with prosecutors.

Police "were told that in January," John said in the series. "They kept that secret from the media and from the District Attorney for months."

Stranger still, investigative reporter Woodward observed in the series, was that the info didn't leak to the media.

"DNA results often leak in murder cases," she said, "yet when the one piece of evidence that clears them, or at least clears their DNA, comes back, there's not a leak about it."

But, Woodward noted, early in the investiation there was "massive police leaking that Patsy Ramsey had written the ransom note." (The theory was duly reported on; multiple handwriting experts determined her writing and the letter did not match, retired Det. Whitson recalled in the series.)

"They kept that secret," John said of the DNA findings, "because it conflicted with their conclusion that we were the killers."

Boulder Police Det. Steve Thomas took over leading the investigation into JonBenét's death in early 1997 and he zeroed in on her parents. In his 2000 book, JonBenét: Inside the Ramsey Murder Investigation, he detailed his theory that Patsy killed her daughter in a rage after the 6-year-old wet the bed, staged the scene in the basement and wrote the ransom note.

He also said this to Patsy and John's faces on an episode of CNN's Larry King Live. They vehemently pushed back, Patsy ultimately saying, "God knows [what happened], and the truth is going to prevail." (The Ramseys filed an $80 million defamation lawsuit against Thomas and his publisher in 2001; it was settled for an undisclosed sum.)

In the Netflix series, John said that Steve's theory "didn't pass the sanity test."

"Patsy had just recovered from stage 4 ovarian cancer," John said. "She was grateful to be alive. Do you think that her child wetting her bed would be a big deal? No. She was happy to be alive and to have some more time with her children."

Steve Thomas resigned from the case in protest in August 1998, accusing the district attorney's office of mishandling the Ramsey case.

In a 2004 interview, Boulder County District Attorney Alex Hunter reflected on "a split" between his office and Boulder PD, noting, "Some Boulder Police people thought they knew who did it. And some of my people were convinced that it was an intruder that did it."

In 1997, the DA's office brought in retired detective Lou Smit to consult on the case. Smit died in 2010, but he detailed in video and audio diaries sampled in the Netflix series why he believed the Ramseys were innocent.

There was "no motive, no evidence of bad character," he said in a 1998 recording, per the series. "There is evidence of an intruder. I say this over and over and over again. Nobody wants to listen."

So when prosecutors opted to take their case against the Ramseys to the grand jury in September 1998, Smit tendered his resignation from the case.

"He would have no part in trying to convict an innocent couple," Colorado Springs Police Department Investigations Commander Kurt Pillar, who considered Smit a mentor, said in the Netflix series. "That's how strongly he felt about this case."

John recalled in the series, "We fully expected and were prepared to be indicted. 'Cause they were saying, 'You can indict a ham sandwich in front a grand jury,' it's a one-sided argument."

More than a year later, District Attorney Hunter announced on Oct. 13, 1999, that his office didn't have the evidence to file charges against the Ramseys—or anyone—at that time.

He did not share the grand jury's recommendation with the public. "I feel at peace and to some extent proud of the fact that I weathered the storm and did the right thing," Hunter said in 2004, "based on the evidence."

In 2008, his successor Mary Lacy publicly exonerated John, Patsy and Burke, citing the results of new touch DNA analysis. "To the extent that we may have contributed in any way to the public perception that you might have been involved in this crime, I am deeply sorry," the DA wrote in a letter to John, per NBC News.

It wasn't until 2013 that the indictment was unsealed, revealing that the grand jury chose to indict John and Patsy on two counts each of child abuse resulting in death. Per the Denver Post, the document didn't accuse them of killing their daughter, but rather of permitting her to be placed in a dangerous situation that led to her death and of assisting a person who "committed and was suspected of the crime of murder in the first degree and child abuse resulting in death."

"We didn't know who did what," a member of the grand jury told the Boulder Daily Camera in January 2013. "But we felt the adults in the house may have done something that they certainly could have prevented, or they could have helped her, and they didn't."

After the 1999 indictment was revealed, Boulder Police Chief Mark Beckner said in a statement that it proved "the investigation pursued by the Boulder Police Department was, in fact, based on the information and evidence available."

"There are no new leads," the statement continued. "While we believe at this point it is unlikely there will ever be a prosecution, the Boulder Police Department still holds out some hope that one day the district attorney and the Boulder Police Department will be able to put together a case worthy of presenting to a jury."

The Ramseys' attorney Lin Wood said in 2013, per the Post, that the grand jury's decision in 1999 was "based on incomplete evidence."

“It’s subject to the impression that criminal charges were warranted against the Ramseys," he said. "A full examination of the evidence unquestionably exonerates the Ramseys. This is inflicting a terrible miscarriage of justice."

#806. The Fifa hopeful hoping to take Infantino down with 'samurai spirit'

Kozo Tashima is under no illusions it will be easy to take down Gianni Infantino - but the first serious challenger for the Fifa presidency says he will draw on his "samurai spirit".

First, the 68-year-old needs to get the endorsement of five member associations around the world.

The honorary president of the Japan Football Association said he has had "good replies" from those he has contacted since announcing his ambition to run in the March elections.

If he achieves the necessary endorsements, the next step is an altogether different proposition - toppling Infantino, who has been in charge of Fifa for a decade and told BBC Sport last month he believed he had the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football.

Tashima, who sits on the Fifa Council, acknowledged the scale of the challenge, but wants to bring "good change" to the organisation.

The former footballer says he is driven by disappointment in Infantino's recent actions, surrounding the cancelled suspension of United States forward Folarin Balogun at the World Cup and the abandoned plan to sell stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

In an exclusive interview with BBC Sport, he spoke of why he feels he cannot leave Fifa as it is.

"I know [Infantino] has a lot of supporters," he said. "Now I am alone and my budget is not enough but it is OK. My policy, my philosophy, I have to fight against him with my samurai spirit.

"I would like to make sure that the game of football is safeguarded and to be loved and enjoyed by everybody. We have to review the system in Fifa and build good governance.

"In the uncertain situation of the world, sports - especially football - can present good values like fair play, co-operation, hard work, integrity, and show the model of the society. So, first to review and rebuild good governance and make football accessible for all with the principle of football first."

Japan's Tashima to stand against Infantino for Fifa presidency

Fifa to share 'key documents' over World Cup sell-off plan

Infantino says he is backed by 'vast majority'

Asked how confident he was in his ability to get the five endorsements, he said: "I have confidence. I already asked to some of the member association and [received] good replies so far."

He laughed when asked if he realistically hopes to win the election in Morocco in March, before saying: "Of course, of course yes, I hope I will win. It is not easy."

Tashima's campaign will centre on his philosophy for the role of Fifa president, which he described as one based on the "values of sincerity, soundness, fair play, and integrity".

Regarding the Balogun red-card incident, which involved US President Donald Trump calling Infantino to ask for the ban to be reviewed, Tashima said: "I have never seen the red card and the next game who can play.

"This is, I hope, never happens in the world football. He didn't explain about this issue, how to come and how [it came] to happen.

He added: "Most of the things are not answered yet by Mr President Infantino.

"With my experience in Japan Football Association, Asian Football Confederation, and Fifa, for some more than 20 years, I would like to bring good change if I am elected."

Last month, former Tottenham Hotspur defender Ramon Vega announced his intention to stand as a candidate in next year's Fifa presidential election.

He told BBC Sport he had received "more than five" endorsements, but declined to give details of the identities of the member associations backing him.

All candidates must prove they have played an "active role" in football for two of the last five years. Vega has said he is confident he is eligible to stand for the presidency as a shareholder of a club.

Vega has attempted to run for the presidency three times before but each time has failed to garner the necessary support of five associations.

Tashima can therefore be considered the first serious challenger to Infantino.

#805. Chelsea’s Alonso identity still to form in a midfield that remains a problem

Roméo Lavia’s resurgence is not enough as injuries to other key players such as Moisés Caicedo are proving disruptive

Xabi Alonso played for Pep Guardiola at Bayern Munich and was a key figure for Spain when their midfield dominated international football between 2008 and 2012. He does not need to be educated about the importance of control, but there has been a clear distinction between his identity as a player and how his Chelsea side have played.

Chelsea’s average possession stands at 47.8% after nine league games. They have made the eighth-most passes in the Premier League and are at their most dangerous on the counterattack. Give them space and they will run riot, but Alonso is yet to see a complete performance and knows they need to improve in midfield.

It is a problem area. Reece James has been out with a knee injury since September and the engine room lacks consistency. Alonso has experimented with different partnerships but is yet to settle on his favoured lineup and will be forced into another change if Chelsea find themselves without Moisés Caicedo when they visit Sunderland on Sunday afternoon.

The Ecuadorian, who has already had a spell on the sidelines with a calf injury, has not trained fully after feeling discomfort this week. It is a complication for Alonso, who keeps having to deal with injuries to key players. The striker João Pedro is out with a thigh injury, the centre-back Maxence Lacroix is hamstrung and there will have to be further adjustment if Caicedo cannot prove his fitness before Chelsea face the league’s bottom side.

Jordan Henderson is the obvious replacement for Caicedo. Chelsea could require the former’s experience given Sunderland probably need to turn the game into a battle, although they will also need poise in possession and are likely to get it from Roméo Lavia, whose elegance would make him an ideal in Alonso’s system if only it could be guaranteed his body was not going to let him down again.

We have been here before with Lavia, who has had little luck since joining from Southampton three years ago. The Belgium international barely played during his first season at Chelsea and has had plenty of false dawns since. The potential is not in doubt; the uncertainty is whether Lavia can stay fit.

Chelsea have not given up on the 22-year-old. Lavia has the talent to reach the top, but is he durable enough? He had not completed a full 90 minutes for Chelsea before going the distance during the Carabao Cup shootout defeat at Liverpool 10 days ago. That speaks volumes and is the reason for the caution, even though Lavia managed another 90 minutes when he produced a dominant display next to Caicedo during Chelsea’s 2-0 win against Manchester United last weekend.

Alonso needs more. He said Lavia had made changes to his physical preparation this season. “There has been a change,” Alonso said, although he did not elaborate. There is no suggestion Lavia has lacked professionalism. He is sensible, driven and smart. The suspicion is that it is more about being efficient from a conditioning perspective. Get that element right and Chelsea will have a top midfielder.

“Every time that the midfield area works, the team works better,” Alonso said. “We saw that Rom is in a very good place. I think that for the last month he has been very consistent in his performances, and he has been very important for the team, because in the middle you need to have a brain not just for yourself but a brain for the team.

“He’s good with the ball, he’s giving balance, he’s connecting very well with the players around him, with through balls. We need to push him, to help to continue, that it’s not enough, that he can take the next step. It’s not rocket science to know once you have good midfielders the team normally looks better.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Alonso needs that conductor to complement Caicedo’s power and ability to put out fires. Chelsea’s manager had Granit Xhaka knitting everything together when Bayer Leverkusen won the Bundesliga in 2024. It was not a surprise when Alonso tried to sign the Sunderland midfielder this summer.

“We spoke a lot in that time in Leverkusen with Granit because he was a key part of that team,” Alonso said. “He glued many pieces together.”

Chelsea are looking for similar cohesion. Alonso is yet to place his trust in Valentín Barco, signed from Strasbourg in the summer. The midfield is incomplete after the £125m sale of Enzo Fernández to Manchester City. A move for Monaco’s Lamine Camara broke down on deadline day and Bournemouth refused to sell Alex Scott after receiving inquiries from Arsenal, Chelsea and Liverpool for the newly capped England midfielder.

The situation will be revisited in January. Chelsea, who also like Crystal Palace’s Adam Wharton, are thought to have the edge over Liverpool in the race to sign Scott. They need to give Alonso more options in midfield. Lavia’s resurgence is not enough. Injuries elsewhere are disrupting Alonso’s plans, preventing him from making Chelsea consistent.

#804. The Fate of Nobody Wants This Revealed After Season 3

Weeks after season three of Nobody Wants This premiered on Netflix, the streaming platform shared whether the series starring Kristen Bell and Adam Brody is renewed for a fourth season.

As it turns out, everybody wants more Kristen Bell and Adam Brody.

Following the success of season three of Nobody Wants This, Netflix confirmed the romantic comedy was renewed for a fourth season.

The exciting news was also confirmed by Bell, who shared on Instagram Nov. 6 that “season 4 is coming” alongside a clip from season three—in which Brody’s character proposes—of her and fellow costars Justine Lupe and Timothy Simons excitedly celebrating.

The show’s creator Erin Foster was also overjoyed by the news, resharing the video to her Instagram Story with the caption, “It’s official.”

She and her fellow producers Jenni Konner and Bruce Eric Kaplan shared their excitement in a Nov. 6 press release from Netflix, joking, “We are so happy and thrilled to do another season of our favorite show on television, which coincidentally is the one we run.”

And the show is extra special for Foster as she was inspired to create Nobody Wants This based on her own experiences with husband Simon Tikhman. In fact, season three’s proposal episode was actually inspired by how Tikhman proposed to her in 2019, fake wedding and all.

“About a month before he proposed,” Foster narrated an Oct. 28 Instagram video, “we got this invitation to a wedding vow renewal. It had attire and a schedule for the whole weekend.”

And while Foster flew to Napa Valley fully expecting to attend a wedding, she was instead surprised by a proposal, as well as both her and Tikhman’s families jumping out to celebrate after hiding in a barn during the proposal.

Still, the 44-year-old—who shares daughter Noa, 2, with Tikhman—has been conscious of how much of her actual life she includes in the series.

“I always have to be careful to not think that everything that happens in my life and my relationship is going to translate and be right for a script,” Foster shared with The Hollywood Reporter in 2025, “and the best way to figure that out is really in the writers' room.”

#803. Newcastle's Dedic stopped by police after being spotted with bow and arrows

Amar Dedic has featured in seven Premier League games since joining Newcastle in August

Newcastle United defender Amar Dedic was stopped by police after being spotted carrying a bow and arrows at a Northumberland beauty spot.

Bosnia-Herzegovina international Dedic, 24, was with a friend when he was stopped in a car after a concerned member of the public raised the alarm.

Reports say six police cars, external were dispatched, including armed police, and that Dedic and his companion were stopped about seven miles away from where they were originally spotted.

Police searched the car and seized the bow and arrows but were satisfied the two men were not a threat to the public.

BBC Sport has been told Dedic had no ill intention and has fully co-operated with police.

It is reported Newcastle goalkeeper Mark Gillespie, 34, and former defender Paul Dummett, 35, arrived at the scene while police were speaking to Dedic.

It is understood the pair were in the area by chance and stopped to offer assistance.

The incident happened on Wednesday, two days after Dedic - who joined from Benfica for a fee in the region of Â£30m in August - had played in Newcastle's 1-0 home defeat by Everton.

Newcastle, who are 13th in the Premier League table on 11 points from nine games, have not commented.

Northumbria Police has released a statement and said enquiries are ongoing. The force has not named Dedic.

It said it received reports of two men carrying a bow and arrows while walking along a track by the reservoir on Military Road in the Harlow Hill area.

"Officers attended and subsequently stopped a vehicle in the Darras Hall area and seized a bow and arrows," added the statement.

"At this stage, it is understood they were for recreational use and there was no threat to the public."

Newcastle are at Fulham on Saturday (15:00 GMT) before the November international break.

Dedic, who has featured in 10 league and cup games since joining Newcastle, has been named in the Bosnia-Herzegovina squad for Nations League matches away to Sweden on 14 November and at home to Romania on 17 November.

#802. ‘A footballing alien’: Mamadou Sangaré soars to Premier League heights

Brentford’s Mali midfielder stood out when he was six and has shone in the Premier League since £39m transfer

“When I first saw him, I thought to myself: ‘Who on earth is this player?’ laughs Youness Bengelloun as he remembers Mamadou Sangaré. With the transfer window in full swing in July 2025, the former Manchester City scout and agent was not expecting to come face to face with a “footballing alien”, but that proved the case during a visit to Rapid Vienna’s training ground. A few weeks later, Sangaré moved to Lens for around €5m. “He was impressive and what struck me was his technique and his work rate,” Bengelloun says.

That’s more or less the impression Sangaré has made at every club he’s played for, including Brentford, for whom the Mali midfielder signed, from Lens, for a club-record £39m at the start of August. The 24-year-old excelled in his debut against Tottenham a few weeks later, dominating the centre of the pitch and providing the assist for Keane Lewis-Potter’s opening goal, and has featured in every game this season, with Brighton up next. “I gave him his debut for Mali in September 2024, against Mozambique. He made an immediate impact,” says Sangaré’s former international manager Tom Saintfiet. “He’s every manager’s dream player.”

Sangaré’s rise began at Association Sportive Aboubacar Coulibaly (ASAC). A small club based in the Faladié neighbourhood of Bamako, Mali’s capital, became a home from home at the age of six. Even then, his strength of character, work ethic and desire to succeed were clear, and immediately impressed his coach at the time, Bakary Coulibaly. “He lived not far from the ASAC pitch, so he’d come and play every day,” Coulibaly says. “Right from the start I could see that Mamadou had great potential. He played as a right midfielder and was already technically better than the others.

“What surprised me most about Mamadou was that he always wanted to win. Even then he was very demanding of himself and his teammates and acted like a leader. When the team was struggling he was always looking for a solution to help us win.”

Setting high standards and taking personal responsibility are sides of Sangaré that Saintfiet recognises. “He manages everything in his professional life,” says the 53-year-old Belgian. “He controls his time for eating, sleeping, training … some people go to nightclubs to clear their heads, but he lives like a professional 24 hours a day.

“I remember one day, Yves Bissouma asked Mamadou what his favourite position on the pitch was. Mamadou answered that he wanted his own. I’ll never forget that moment because it shows he had enormous confidence in his own abilities. But he’s not arrogant; he’s very shy. Very laid-back.”

Saintfiet, who managed Mali from 2024 to 2026, adds: “When I think of Mamadou, I think first and foremost of his personality. He’s never nervous, he always stays calm. He’s always in control of the situation. When he receives the ball surrounded by three players, he’ll keep his cool and he’ll manage to find the pass to get out of it”.

Sangaré progressed from ASAC to Yeelen Olympique before leaving Mali for Europe in September 2020, joining RB Salzburg after catching the eye of scouts from the Austrian club via video footage. There came various loan spells before a permanent move to Rapid Vienna in July 2024, and then on to Lens the following August, with Sangaré’s one and only season at the French club a memorable one. Not only did he play a key role in Lens winning the Coupe de France but, in the process, he also picked up the Marc-Vivien Foé award, which recognises the best African player in Ligue 1.

Last season Sangaré took part in his first Africa Cup of Nations, where he helped Mali reach the quarter-finals. “The match during which he was the most impressive was against the Comoros [in the group stages],” says his fellow Mali midfielder, Lassana Coulibaly. “The first time we had seen him in training we all noticed he had that extra something. But in that match he was absolutely incredible”.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Saintfiet was impressed with Sangaré’s performance against the hosts Morocco, also in the group stage, and especially by his attitude beforehand. “I asked him to play on the right flank so we could field five midfielders. When you ask certain players to play in different positions, they often tell you it’s not their natural role and that they don’t feel comfortable. But when I spoke to Mamadou about it he immediately said: ‘OK coach, I’ll play wherever you want for the good of the team. I’ll do my best. He is a loyal player who has always done everything he could to help me.”

Brentford are the latest recipients of Sangaré’s capabilities, on and off the pitch, and Saintfiet is sure they won’t be the last. “I reckon he can play at an even higher level,” he says. “He won’t stop at Brentford.”

#801. Daily briefing: Toothbrush zaps bacteria to clear plaque

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

Paediatrician Annie Andrews, a Democrat, won a US Senate seat in South Carolina in a surprise victory on 3 November. Democrats had not won a Senate seat in the state since 1998.Credit: Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc/Getty

The US mid-term elections won the Democratic party power in both chambers of the US Congress, raising hopes that lawmakers will now push back against disruptions to science introduced by the administration of Republican President Donald Trump. Democratic majorities in both the House and Senate will give the party the power to craft legislation that counteracts Trump’s science agenda. But the President could still veto these bills, since Democrats don’t hold more than two-thirds of seats in either chamber. The results have also brought a wave of scientists and medical professionals into political office. “The nerds strike back,” says Shaughnessy Naughton, president of the political fundraising group 314 Action.

A new manual toothbrush can destroy bacteria by generating its own electrical charge, rather than relying on friction alone. The brush’s bristles are made from a polymer that researchers stretched and heated to obtain its piezoelectric form — meaning it generates a charge when deformed. During brushing, the bending bristles release charges that create highly reactive forms of oxygen in nearby saliva. These damage bacteria cell membranes, the team says. When the bristles relax, the material reabsorbs the charges, ready to go again.

Two new studies analysing more than 4,700 ancient human genomes have identified the possible origins of Celtic and Germanic languages and found migrations that might have dispersed their speakers around Europe. The findings could explain why Germanic languages such as English and Dutch are so widespread, whereas Celtic languages such as Welsh and Gaelic are concentrated to a few million people in northern Europe.

Three people with drug-resistant epilepsy saw the number of seizures they had per month fall by more than 90%, after gene-laden viruses were infused into their brains as part of an early-stage clinical trial. The treatment was targeted to the small patch of brain tissue responsible for each participants’ seizures. The virus carried a gene that made neurons in that area sensitive to clozapine, a drug that activates the gene therapy, which in turn helps to suppress the abnormal electrical activity associated with seizures. The participants didn’t experience any serious side effects, but long-term use of clozapine might bring cardiovascular risks and other problems, say researchers.

Reference: New England Journal of Medicine paper

A genetics lab in Shanghai has handed almost all control over to a team of robots guided by artificial-intelligence agents. The robotic arms in the ‘self-driving’ lab can operate more than 20 types of instrument, complete thousands of operations in a single project and see through experiments that involve synthesizing and sequencing DNA, among other tasks. The system, called ‘AutoDNA’, uses a simple human prompt to design and execute experiments. While it’s running, human hands are required only to refresh reagents and service hardware.

Health information distributed as part of a randomized clinical trial can unintentionally reshape social relationships, as demonstrated by a trial in rural Honduras. Researchers found that the intervention — which involved being provided with information about child and maternal health — affected people’s friendships, financial relationships and whom they went to for health advice. In villages where only a few people received the information, overall connectivity decreased, whereas it increased in places where the intervention covered the majority of households. (Nature News & Views | 6 min read)

When NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins launched on a SpaceX capsule to the International Space Station last month, she became the first Black woman to command a crewed space mission. Sian Proctor, the first Black woman to pilot a spacecraft (on a private SpaceX mission in 2021) reflects on how commercial spaceflight is increasing access and how Watkins’s accomplishment might help lead us to a future in space that reflects the people on Earth.

Space.com | 11 min read (free registration required)

Research into Parkinson’s disease has historically focussed on the brain, and the processes that lead to the death of dopamine neurons the disorder causes. But this research hasn’t yet pinpointed a genetic component of the disease in most people, leaving its underlying trigger unknown. Now, some researchers are investigating environmental factors that could contribute to disease onset, and others have found evidence that changes to proteins in the gut could precede symptoms in the brain.

This article is part of Nature Outlook: Parkinson’s disease, a supplement produced with financial support from Aspen Neuroscience, Inc.

Within a decade, humanity will know whether artificial-intelligence tools will enable “radical abundance” or “society being torn apart”, says computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton — who won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2024 for his work in developing tools for understanding the neural networks that underpin AI. (The Guardian | 5 min read)

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03596-w

Today I’m pondering the best name for a space-cleaning robot. No, this isn’t just a silly thought experiment — the UK Space Agency (UKSA) is holding a competition to name their space debris clean-up mission. The agency is calling for maximum two-word names that fit the theme of “a name inspired by keeping space clean and safe for future generations”.

The UKSA has helpfully provided some examples of the names of past missions as inspiration — and perhaps to steer people away from the joke suggestions that have topped naming polls in the UK before.

Let us know what you’d suggest, along with any feedback on this newsletter, at briefing@nature.com.

Jacob Smith, associate editor, Nature Briefing

#800. Why Russell Brand, Katy Perry Marriage Was Not Mentioned in Rape Trial

Russell Brand was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault in London court. See why the disgraced comedian’s former marriage to Katy Perry was not included in arguments.

Katy Perry’s history with Russell Brand was not included in his rape trial.

After the disgraced comedian was found guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault in London’s Southwark Crown Court, the prosecution confirmed why Brand’s 14-month marriage to Perry in 2010 was not part of their opening arguments.

“The prosecution recognize that matters post 2009 involving his relationship with Katy Perry may be sensitive,” lead prosecutor Riel Karmy-Jones KC said in a pre-trial submissions statement, per The Telegraph, “as may his previous faiths, and we are content to remove these from the opening.”

Similarly, the “Teenage Dream” singer—now mom to a 6-year-old daughter with ex Orlando Bloom—was not asked to provide any kind of witness statement during the police investigation into Brand.

While Perry was not involved in the investigation or trial—which included allegations of events that occurred between 2004 and 2009, the same year Brand and Perry started dating—in any way, Brand briefly mentioned his relationship to the Grammy nominee while testifying during the trail, sharing how he achieved “staggering fame” at that time in his life.

Following the guilty verdict, the Forgetting Sarah Marshall alum—who was cleared of two separate counts of rape as well as one count of indecent assault—was told by presiding judge Joel Bennathan that he plans to sentence the actor to “significant custodial time,” while also denying him bail. Brand’s sentencing is set to take place on Monday, Nov. 9.

E! News reached out to Brand’s attorneys for comment, as well as his and Perry’s representatives, but has not yet heard back.

In the years since his marriage to Perry, Brand—father to three kids with wife Laura Brand—has reemerged in the public eye as a right-winged Christian influencer. And he has acknowledged his faith while denying the allegations against him.

“I pray Lord, anyone that I’ve harmed or hurt in my years of mindlessness and sin would be healed, Lord,” he said in a 2025 video shared to social media. “And I pray, Lord, for the absolute truth of who I am to be abundantly revealed.”

For her part, Perry has been extremely open with the emotional toll her relationship with Brand took on her following their divorce being finalized in 2012.

"My self-worth was in someone else's hands, which is never a good idea, because it can be taken from you at any time," she told The Sunday Times at the time. "And it was, and it was shattered. But I don't do that anymore.”

#799. Has Anderson lived up to the hype after Man City move?

Elliot Anderson started his career at Newcastle before moves to Nottingham Forest and Manchester City

Elliot Anderson's stock has risen astronomically and there were considerable expectations on the midfielder's shoulders after sealing a Â£116m move from Nottingham Forest to Manchester City in the summer.

The 24-year-old established himself as one of the best players in the Premier League and has become a key man for England, helping Thomas Tuchel's side to a third-placed finish at this summer's World Cup.

His highly impressive performances for Forest over the past two seasons had him tracked by the likes of Manchester United and Arsenal before his move to Etihad Stadium.

European football expert Guillem Balague said on BBC Match of the Day he had spoken to City manager Enzo Maresca in the summer and asked if he wants to sign Bournemouth's Alex Scott and Crystal Palace's Adam Wharton.

The Italian's response was "no", adding: "Anderson is going to become the key player for England, not just City."

Anderson may well be afforded a generous reception when he makes his return to the City Ground on Saturday, with Forest supporter Ellie Molloson telling BBC Sport: "I know the stadium will be ringing with 'Geordie Maradona'.

"It will be bittersweet because we miss him, but we are quite proud of just how fantastic a player he is."

Few Forest fans will "begrudge him for his whopping move", but is Anderson managing to live up to the hype in the early days of his City career?

Anderson was one of the standout central midfielders in the Premier League last season.

He topped the rankings for a number of metrics such as touches of the ball, winning possession, contesting duels and drawing the most fouls.

His influence was striking despite featuring in a struggling Forest side which had four different managers and finished only five points above the relegation zone.

The former Newcastle player's tireless work-rate means he has effectively replaced Bernardo Silva and Rodri at City, making the step up to a side that won two trophies last season and could challenge for the title again.

Though Anderson has not fully replicated the outright league-leading dominance he showcased across several metrics last season, his underlying numbers remain elite.

He has drawn more fouls (28) than any other player in the division, while he ranks second for duels won (66) and third for successful passes (610) and touches on the ball (851).

Only Tottenham's Jan Paul van Hecke and Arsenal's Declan Rice have managed more successful passes in the opposition half and line-breaking passes than Anderson, but the City midfielder has played at least 66 minutes fewer than both.

Anderson's deep-lying number six role means he has only one goal and two assists in 14 games this season, though he did lay on Erling Haaland's winner against RB Leipzig in the Champions League on Wednesday.

"He has been amazing," said Haaland afterwards. "He has had an amazing start to his City career and that is what you expect. You have to come straight in and perform.

"It is not easy to come in, you need to adapt and new players and a new coach, so he he has been impressive. Respect."

Elliot Anderson a 'potential legend' at Man City

In Tuesday's training session open to the media before City's trip to Leipzig, some players came out looking relaxed in groups but Anderson emerged by himself, doing kick-ups with a laser focus on the ball.

It perhaps hints at a steely determination to remain fixated and give his best at every opportunity, whether that be in training or during the intensity of a match.

Anderson was the first to step up in one of the group drills and was deemed the winner during a set-up which involved a slalom with the ball before smashing a finish into a mini net.

Asked if he was surprised at how quickly Anderson had settled in to life at City, Maresca told BBC Sport: "Knowing him now, he is a guy who wants to learn every day and we sat with him with video [analysis].

"He wants to understand things, he wants to learn and improve and for a manager it's a dream because you know that he wants to learn and you can do different things."

Molloson adds: "The way Anderson reads the game, the way he dominates midfield, he is such an intelligent football player and he is so young, there is still so much more to come from him.

"He is a leader on the pitch and I just think he is phenomenal. I think Forest fans would definitely have him back in a heartbeat."

Maresca has acknowledged Anderson's box-to-box qualities but sees him as City's number six this season. The demands of this role differ from how Anderson has previously been used.

Following Manchester City's 4â1 win over Crystal Palace in August, Anderson said: "I'm loving [my role but] it's a bit different to what I've been used to. I've got to be a bit more structured, that's what I'm learning, to stay in my position. At Forest I was doing a little bit more."

His physicality, intensity and intelligence make him an excellent front-footed midfielder, capable of pressing players high or wide, winning the ball and starting attacks. When City have pressed man-to-man but been played through, Anderson has often impressively stopped attacks alone.

Brighton launch a dangerous counter-attack but Anderson impressively wins the ball back

Anderson's value in a more expansive role was seen in his assist for Haaland's winner at Leipzig this week, as he drove with the ball before playing a cross, reminiscent of Kevin de Bruyne.

Although City's holding midfielder, Anderson's skillset makes him effective across the pitch

The same qualities that Anderson posesses have also been exploited at times.

Habitually, he reacts to players more than thinking about positions, as he is able to win the ball back more often than not from most players. As a result, some opponents have looked to position themselves near him before moving away, enticing the Englishman to follow.

Sunderland's Enzo le Fee made constant off-the-ball runs around and beyond Anderson in September. The England midefielder, almost magnetically, locked on to Le Fee, tracking those runs, which left space in front of City's defence.

Paris St-Germain and Brighton also used these decoy runs to pull Anderson away, creating space in midfield.

Here is an example of Le Fee using Anderson's front-footedness against him. By dropping deep and wide, Le Fee entices Anderson to follow him, vacating his holding midfield position

This opens up space in the centre of the pitch for Sunderland to find their striker, Brian Brobbey, in one pass

Ayyoub Bouaddi has been trialled alongside Anderson in midfield. When Anderson does vacate the holding midfield position to press, something we saw against PSG, a second defensive midfielder alongside him can help protect the centre of the pitch â a temporary fix as Anderson moulds his impressive skillset to Maresca's asks.

In 2021, Guardiola reflected on Rodri's first season, saying: "Last season he moved too much. The holding midfielder has to be there, don't move, be there." In 2024, he won the Ballon d'Or.

City will certainly be pleased with the quality of Anderson so far. It would also be fair to say his debut season has begun better than Rodri's did in 2020. But both City and Anderson will be hoping for a development in positional understanding that mimics the player he was brought in to replace.

Maresca's big test is to address mounting Man City issues
